saarbrucken: Saarbrücken lies on the Saar, a tributary of the Moselle, and directly borders the French department of Moselle. Two origins are proposed for the second part of its name: the Celtic brigā, meaning hill or rock, since the castle of Sarabrucca stood on a large rock above the river, or the Old High German brucca, meaning bridge or corduroy road, since a ford lay beside the castle. The modern city was formed in 1909 by the merger of Saarbrücken, now called Alt-Saarbrücken, St Johann and Malstatt-Burbach.

The Mediomatrici settled the area in the last centuries BCE, and Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul brought it into the Roman Empire. The Alemanni destroyed the Gallo-Roman settlement of vicus Saravus toward the end of the fourth century. The oldest document naming the town is a deed of 999 by which Emperor Otto III gave the castellum Sarabrucca to the Bishops of Metz, who granted the area to the Counts of Saargau as a fief. In 1321 or 1322 Count Johann I of Saarbrücken-Commercy gave town status to Saarbrücken and the fishing village of St Johann. From 1381 to 1793 the counts of Nassau-Saarbrücken were the main local rulers.

The Thirty Years' War cut the population from 4,500 in 1628 to 70 by 1637, and in 1677 Louis XIV's troops burned the town, leaving eight houses standing. Under Prince William Henry (1741–1768) the coal mines were nationalised, and the architect Friedrich Joachim Stengel built the Friedenskirche, the Old City Hall and, in 1775, the Ludwigskirche. After 1815 the town belonged to the Prussian Rhine Province, and coal and iron were developed, with the Burbach ironworks opening in 1856.

Saarbrücken was the capital of the Territory of the Saar Basin from 1920, when the Treaty of Versailles gave France the Saar's coal mines for fifteen years; in 1935 more than 90 per cent voted to rejoin Germany. Bombing in the Second World War killed 1,234 people and left 75 per cent of the city in ruins. France later made the Saar a protectorate with Saarbrücken as its capital, and in a referendum in 1955 over two thirds rejected an independent Saar state. The territory rejoined West Germany in 1957.

Saarbrücken is the capital and largest city of Saarland, with about 180,000 inhabitants. Its landmarks include the stone bridge of the 16th century, the Gothic church of St Arnual and the 18th-century castle. It is the seat of Saarland University and of the administration of the Franco-German University.
saarland: Saarland is a landlocked state in the south-west of Germany, with an area of 2,570 km2, about the same as neighbouring Luxembourg. It is bordered by the French department of Moselle to the south and west, by Rhineland-Palatinate to the north and east, and by a short stretch of Luxembourg. It is named after the river Saar, a tributary of the Moselle. A third of the land is forest, and the state is generally hilly. Most inhabitants live in a city agglomeration on the French border around the capital, Saarbrücken.

The region was settled by the Celtic Treveri and Mediomatrici, whose most impressive relic is the fortress of refuge at Otzenhausen. Roman rule ended in the 5th century when the Franks conquered the territory, and for the next 1,300 years the region shared the history of the Kingdom of the Franks, the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, divided into small territories. French kings invaded in 1635, 1676, 1679 and 1734 and founded Saarlouis in 1680. The armies of the French Revolution ended the territories' independence after 1792, and in 1815 most of the region went to the Prussian Rhine Province. Coal and heavy industry gave it importance in the 19th century.

It became a distinct political entity in 1920 as the Territory of the Saar Basin, governed by France under a League of Nations mandate. In the plebiscite of 13 January 1935, 90.8 percent of those voting favoured rejoining Germany. After the Second World War it became the Saar Protectorate under French occupation on 17 December 1947. A plebiscite on 23 October 1955 rejected the Saar Statute, which would have made it independent, and it joined West Germany on 1 January 1957. The Saar franc remained its currency until 7 July 1959.

Saarland has about one million inhabitants and is the smallest German state in area apart from the city-states of Berlin, Bremen and Hamburg. Saarbrücken is its capital and largest city. Coal mining, for 250 years a mainstay of its economy, ended with the closure of the last mine in 2012, and the Völklingen Ironworks is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its people speak Rhine Franconian and Moselle Franconian dialects, and French has a special standing in its schools.
sadashivrao-bhau: Sadashivrao Bhau was born on 4 August 1730 at Satara into a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family, the son of Chimaji Appa, younger brother of Peshwa Baji Rao I, and Rakhmabai of the Pethe family. His mother died when he was about a month old and his father when he was ten, and he was raised by his grandmother Radhabai and his aunt Kashibai. He served as a finance minister during the reign of the Maratha ruler Rajaram II.

His first campaign was in Karnataka in 1746. He won his first battle at Ajra, south of Kolhapur, and took thirty-six parganas. In a later Carnatic campaign he conquered territory from the Nawab of Savanur and put down the revolt of Yamaji Shivdev.

Having seen the effect of artillery and light guns in British hands, he built similar units for the Maratha army. In 1760 he engaged Ibrahim Khan Gardi, a former officer of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who brought 2,500 trained soldiers and fifteen cannons. Within two years the infantry and artillery division had grown to 10,000 men and 56 guns.

Appointed to lead the army to Delhi against Ahmad Shah Abdali, he set out from Patdur on 14 March 1760 with about 55,000 men and roughly 200,000 non-combatants, including families and pilgrims. Unlike Malharrao Holkar and Raghunathrao he did not know the politics of the north. He disregarded the advice of Suraj Mal, the Jat ruler of Bharatpur, to leave the civilians at Agra. The army took Delhi on 2 August 1760 and then stormed the fort of Kunjpura, killing its entire garrison.

Abdali crossed the swollen Yamuna at Baghpat between 23 and 25 October 1760, surprised the Marathas and cut their supply lines. A two-month blockade near Panipat brought famine to the camp, where many civilians and animals died. On 14 January 1761 the Marathas tried to break out. After his nephew Vishwasrao, the Peshwa's heir, was killed around 2 p.m., Sadashivrao reportedly left his elephant and charged on horseback; the empty howdah led some troops to think him dead. He died fighting, and the remaining civilians were massacred. Some records say his headless body was recovered three days later, others that it was never found.

His widow Parvatibai, who had accompanied the campaign, refused the conventional life of widowhood. Around 1770 a man appeared in Pune claiming to be Sadashivrao; he was exposed and became known as Totayaa, the impostor. The Sadashiv Peth quarter of Pune is named after him.
saddam-hussein: Saddam Hussein al-Majid was born on 28 April 1937 in the village of al-Awja, near Tikrit, to a peasant Sunni Arab family. He joined the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party in 1957. In October 1959 he took part in the attempt to assassinate Prime Minister Abdul-Karim Qasim in Baghdad; he began shooting too early, which disorganised the ambush, and Qasim survived. In July 1968 he took part in the bloodless coup led by Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr, who became president with Saddam as his deputy. As vice president he nationalised the Iraq Petroleum Company and was involved in the Second Iraqi-Kurdish War of 1974 to 1975, in which the Kurds were defeated and hundreds of thousands of Kurdish civilians were forcibly relocated.

On 16 July 1979 Saddam forced the ailing al-Bakr to resign and took the presidency, having long been the de facto leader. Days later he convened a Ba'ath assembly, claimed to have found a fifth column within the party and had 68 alleged conspirators named and arrested; 22 were sentenced to execution. In 1980 he ordered the invasion of Iran, fearing the spread of the Iranian revolution among Iraq's Shia majority. The war ended after nearly eight years in a stalemate, with somewhere around a million lives lost.

When Kuwait refused to waive Iraq's war debt, Saddam accused it of slant-drilling Iraqi oil and occupied it, beginning the Gulf War of 1990 to 1991. A coalition led by the United States defeated Iraq, and the United Nations imposed sanctions. Uprisings of Shia Muslims and Kurds that followed were repressed, and the dead are estimated at 100,000 to 180,000, mostly civilians.

The United States and its allies invaded Iraq on 20 March 2003, accusing Saddam of developing weapons of mass destruction and of ties with al-Qaeda, claims that proved false. Baghdad fell on 9 April, and he was captured on 13 December 2003. He was tried by the Iraqi High Tribunal for the killing of 148 people at Dujail in 1982, convicted on 5 November 2006 of crimes against humanity and sentenced to death by hanging. He was executed on 30 December 2006. Many Arabs praise him as a leader who stood up to Western intervention, while many Iraqis, especially Shias and Kurds, remember a dictator responsible for repression.
sahara: The Sahara covers about 9,200,000 square kilometres, 31 per cent of the African continent, and is the largest hot desert in the world. It stretches from the Red Sea in the east and the Mediterranean in the north to the Atlantic, and excludes the fertile Mediterranean coast, the Atlas Mountains of the Maghreb and the Nile Valley. To the south it is bounded by the Sahel, a belt of semi-arid tropical savanna. The name comes from the Arabic ṣaḥrāʾ, meaning desert.

Its landscape includes hamada, or rocky plateaus, ergs, or sand seas whose dunes often rise over 180 metres, gravel plains, dry valleys called wadis, and salt flats. Mountain massifs rise from it, among them the Ahaggar, the Tibesti and the Aïr, and Emi Koussi in the Tibesti is its highest peak. The central Sahara is hyperarid and may go years without rain, and the Libyan Desert is among the driest and sunniest places on Earth. Trees and taller shrubs grow in the wadis and oases, and the vegetation at the margins is sparse grassland and desert shrub.

For several hundred thousand years the Sahara has alternated between desert and savanna grassland in a cycle of about 20,000 years, caused by the precession of Earth's axis, which shifts the North African monsoon. Scientists have identified more than 230 humid periods in North Africa over the past eight million years. The Green Sahara of the most recent humid period was home to Epipaleolithic, Mesolithic and pastoral peoples, whose rock art survives. The remains of a child at Uan Muhuggiag and of another at Tin Hanakaten have been examined in modern laboratories.

From around 7,500 years ago, populations associated with European Neolithic farmers moved into north-western Africa from the Iberian Peninsula, and pastoralists from the Levant also reached the region. The proto-Berber tribes evolved from these prehistoric communities during the late Bronze and early Iron Ages. Archaeological evidence shows that Nilo-Saharan speaking groups lived in the central and southern Sahara before Berber and Arabic speakers, who now largely populate it, arrived around 1,500 years ago.

The Sahara covers large parts of Algeria, Chad, Egypt, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Western Sahara and Sudan, and parts of southern Morocco and Tunisia. Its peoples include the Amazigh, among them the Tuareg, the Hassaniya-speaking Sahrawis, the Toubou, Nubians, Zaghawa, Kanuri, Hausa, Songhai, Beja and Fulani. The Haratins are believed to descend largely from ancient black populations of the desert. Arabic dialects are the most widely spoken languages, followed by Berber languages and Beja, all of the Afro-Asiatic family. The Richat Structure in Mauritania is among its unusual landforms.
sahel: The Sahel is a biogeographical region of Africa, the transition zone between the more humid Sudanian savannas to the south and the drier Sahara to the north. It spans 5,900 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, in a belt several hundred to a thousand kilometres wide, and has a hot semi-arid climate. The name comes from the Arabic word sāḥil, coast or shore, explained as a figurative reference to the southern edge of the Sahara. Rainfall varies from around 100 to 200 millimetres a year in the north to 700 to 1,000 in the south.

Around 4000 BCE the climate of the Sahara and the Sahel began to dry at great speed. Lakes and rivers shrank and the land became more desert, and farming communities migrated to the more humid climate of West Africa. For hundreds of years the region has had frequent droughts; one megadrought lasted 250 years, from 1450 to 1700. The larger Sahelian kingdoms emerged from 750 CE and founded several large cities in the Niger valley, among them Timbuktu, Gao and Djenné.

In the eastern Sahel the Christian Nubian kingdom of Alodia was first mentioned in 569 and reached its zenith from the 9th to the 12th century; its capital Soba, near present-day Khartoum, was described as a city of extensive dwellings and churches.

With the forest-savanna mosaic to their south, the Sahelian states could not expand into the forest, because mounted warriors were ineffective there and horses and camels were susceptible to the humidity and diseases of the tropics. The western Sahel fell to France in the late 19th century as part of French West Africa, and Chad was added in 1900 as part of French Equatorial Africa. The French territories were decolonised in 1960. The eastern Sahel was conquered by Muhammad Ali of Egypt in the 1820s, came under British rule by 1899 and was granted independence in 1956.

Traditionally most people of the Sahel have been semi-nomads who farm and raise livestock in a system of transhumance, grazing herds in the drier north during the wet season and trekking hundreds of kilometres south in the dry period. Its peoples include the Fulani, Tuareg, Hausa, Dogon, Songhai, Mande, Kanuri and Arabs. Trans-Saharan trade routes and the spread of Islam created strong historical connections between many Sahelian peoples and Arab communities, which influenced language, religion and social customs.
saint-barthelemy: Saint Barthélemy lies about 30 kilometres southeast of Saint Martin, northeast of Saba and Sint Eustatius and north of Saint Kitts and Nevis. It is a volcanic island, encircled by shallow reefs, with an area of 25 square kilometres. Its highest peak is Morne de Vitet, at 286 metres. The climate is essentially arid, and the hills have poor soil that supports mostly cacti and succulent plants. Its capital and main harbour is Gustavia, built in a U-shaped cove on the west coast.

Before European contact the island was possibly visited by Taíno and Arawak people, but it was probably not permanently inhabited because it lacked fresh water. Christopher Columbus was the first European to encounter it, in 1493, and named it in honour of his younger brother Bartholomew Columbus and Bartholomew the Apostle. By 1648 French settlers had arrived, encouraged by Phillippe de Longvilliers de Poincy of the French West India Company, and they began cultivating cacao. Caribs attacked the settlement in 1656 and it was briefly abandoned.

The island proved economically unsuccessful and was troubled by pirates. British forces captured it in 1744 and it returned to French control in 1764. In 1784 King Louis XVI, deeming it of little worth, traded it to Sweden in return for trading privileges in Gothenburg. The Swedes declared Gustavia, named after Gustav III, a free port, which brought prosperity from trade, and built three forts. British forces occupied the island in March 1801, and the outnumbered Swedes surrendered without resistance. It remained a Swedish colony for nearly a century and returned to French rule after a referendum.

On 19 March 1946 the people of the island became French citizens with full rights. For many years it was a commune forming part of Guadeloupe, and in 2003 its voters chose to separate. It became a separate overseas collectivity of France in February 2007. The Three Crowns of the Swedish arms appear in its coat of arms. The language, cuisine and culture are French Caribbean, the euro is the currency, and the economy rests on tourism and duty-free retail.
saint-helena: Saint Helena is a volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean, measuring about 16 by 8 kilometres. It lies some 1,860 kilometres west of Angola and 3,280 kilometres east of Brazil, which makes it one of the most remote major islands in the world. Its climate is mild, tempered by the Benguela Current and almost continuous trade winds. The island is named after Helena of Constantinople.

By long tradition the island was sighted on 21 May 1502 by the four ships of the 3rd Portuguese Armada under João da Nova. A paper of 2022 observed that the only primary sources are Portuguese chronicles written at least fifty years later, none of which gives a precise date. The Portuguese found it uninhabited, with many trees and fresh water, brought livestock and fruit trees, and built a chapel, but formed no permanent settlement. It became a source of food for ships on the Cape Route from Asia to Europe, and sick mariners were left there to recover.

The East India Company received a charter from Oliver Cromwell to govern the island and decided to fortify it and settle it with planters. In 1815 the British government chose Saint Helena as the place of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte after Waterloo. He arrived in October 1815, lived at the Briars pavilion until Longwood House was ready in December, and died at Longwood on 5 May 1821. The Company then resumed control until the India Act of 1833 made the island a crown colony. Dinuzulu, the Zulu king, was exiled there from 1890 to 1897.

Royal Navy ships also brought liberated Africans to the island after rescuing them from slave ships. The remains of some 325 of them, disinterred during airport construction, were stored in Jamestown awaiting reburial.

Saint Helena is one of the three parts of the British overseas territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha, with 4,439 inhabitants at the 2021 census. The island is known for its many endemic birds and plants, over 500 endemic species in all, most of them in the highland cloud forest.
saint-petersburg: Saint Petersburg lies in the middle taiga lowlands along the shores of the Neva Bay of the Gulf of Finland, at the head of the Baltic Sea, and on the islands of the Neva delta. The largest of these are Vasilyevsky Island and Petrogradsky Island. In the south the city crosses the Baltic-Ladoga Klint and meets the Izhora Plateau. Before the 17th century the area was inhabited by the Finnic Izhorians and Votians, and Ingrian Finns moved there from Karelia and Savonia under Swedish rule.

Swedish colonists built the fortress of Nyenskans at the mouth of the Neva in 1611, and the small town of Nyen grew up around it. At the end of the 17th century Peter the Great wanted a seaport to trade with the rest of Europe, since the main one, Arkhangelsk on the White Sea, was closed to shipping in winter. On 12 May 1703 (1 May, old style), during the Great Northern War, he captured Nyenskans. On 27 May 1703 (16 May, old style), he laid down the Peter and Paul Fortress on Zayachy Island, the first brick and stone building of the new city. It was named after the apostle Saint Peter.

The city served as the capital of the Tsardom of Russia and of the Russian Empire from 1712 to 1918, except around 1728 to 1730, when Moscow replaced it. After the October Revolution in 1917 the Bolsheviks moved their government to Moscow. The city was renamed Petrograd and then Leningrad after Lenin's death in 1924. It was the site of the siege of Leningrad in World War II, the most lethal siege in history. In June 1991 voters supported restoring the original name, which took effect on 1 October 1991.

The first Russian railway was built there in 1837. The Kunstkamera, whose collection Peter the Great established in 1714 to gather curiosities from around the world, is sometimes considered the first museum in Russia. In 1914 an international chess tournament, partly funded by Tsar Nicholas II, was the first at which the title Grandmaster was formally conferred, on Lasker, Capablanca, Alekhine, Tarrasch and Marshall.

Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, with 5,601,911 residents in the 2021 census, and is governed as a federal city. Its historic centre, mostly Baroque and Neoclassical buildings of the 18th and 19th centuries, has been largely preserved. The Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The city has more than two hundred museums, the largest being the Hermitage, which occupies the former imperial residence.
sakhalin: Sakhalin is 948 km long and 25 to 170 km wide, with an area of 72,492 square kilometres, and separates the Sea of Okhotsk from the Sea of Japan. Its north coast lies 6.5 km from the Russian mainland across the narrow Strait of Tartary, and its southern tip lies 40 km north of Hokkaido across the La Pérouse Strait. Nearly two thirds of the island is mountainous. The name comes from the Manchu Sahaliyan, meaning black, which is also the Manchu name of the Amur River.

Humans lived on Sakhalin in the Neolithic. The Ainu live in the southern half, the Oroks in the centre and the Nivkhs in the north. The Ainu later paid tribute to the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties, which called the island Kuyedao, the island of the Ainu; control from China was mostly loose and there was no fixed border. Japan proclaimed sovereignty over the whole island in 1845, holding it to be an extension of Hokkaido, against competing Russian claims, and Russian settlers began to establish coal mines, schools and churches.

The Treaty of Shimoda of 1855 allowed nationals of both countries to live on the island, Russians in the north and Japanese in the south, with no clear boundary. Japan surrendered its claims in the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1875 in exchange for the northern Kuril Islands. Under the Treaty of Portsmouth of 1905 Japan received the part south of the 50th parallel, which it governed as Karafuto Prefecture, with its capital at Toyohara, now Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. The Soviet Union invaded southern Sakhalin on 11 August 1945 and completed the conquest on 25 August.

Sakhalin is the largest island of Russia and is administered as part of Sakhalin Oblast. Its population is roughly 500,000, most of them Russians, and the indigenous Ainu, Oroks and Nivkhs are present in very small numbers. Most Ainu on Sakhalin moved to Hokkaido in 1949, when Japanese civilians were displaced from the island.
sakhalin-oblast: Sakhalin Oblast, in the Russian Far East, has an area of 87,100 square kilometres. It borders by sea Khabarovsk Krai to the west and Kamchatka Krai to the north, and Hokkaido in Japan to the south. The name Sakhalin goes back to the Manchu hydronym Sahaliyan Ula, meaning Black River, the Amur. The indigenous peoples of Sakhalin are the Nivkh, Orok and Ainu, the Ainu historically living in the southern part of the island and the Nivkh mainly in the north.

Mamiya Rinzō, who explored and mapped the island in 1809, showed that it is not attached to the Asian continent, and the Russian navigator Gennady Nevelskoy recorded this definitively in 1849. Japan proclaimed sovereignty over the whole island in 1845, but Russian settlers ignored the claim and from the 1850s set up coal mines, prisons and churches. In 1875 the Treaty of Saint Petersburg gave all of it to Russia in exchange for the Kuril Islands, and in 1905 the Treaty of Portsmouth passed the part below 50° N to Japan, which administered it as Karafuto.

In August 1945 the Soviet Union took over the whole of Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, and by 2 January 1947 the present boundaries of the oblast were set. Most Japanese residents were repatriated, but at least a third of the Koreans who had arrived in the late 1930s and early 1940s were refused permission to leave, and they and their descendants became known as the Sakhalin Koreans. Japan does not count the southern Kuril Islands, which it calls the Northern Territories, as included in its renunciation under the Treaty of San Francisco of 1952.

The administrative centre and largest city is Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. The population was 466,609 at the 2021 census, and most inhabitants descend from Russian and other Slavic settlers. Oil and natural gas are drilled on and around the island, and coal and some manganese have been mined there since the 1920s. The 1995 Neftegorsk earthquake killed 1,989 people, and the settlement was not rebuilt.
saladin: Saladin was born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq. His personal name was Yusuf; Salah ad-Din is an honorific meaning Righteousness of the Faith. His parents were of Kurdish Rawadiya ancestry, a tribe originally of Arab descent that had become Kurdicized, and his father Najm al-Din Ayyub was a Kurdish mercenary. His military career began under his paternal uncle Shirkuh, a commander in the service of Nur al-Din. In 1164, aged 26, Saladin went with Shirkuh to Egypt to help restore the vizier Shawar, though his role in that expedition was minor.

Shirkuh and Saladin returned in 1169, when Amalric I of Jerusalem besieged Cairo; Shirkuh became vizier and died the same year, and the Fatimid caliph al-Adid appointed Saladin. In 1171, after al-Adid's death, the Abbasid khutba was pronounced in Cairo, ending the Isma'ili Fatimid Caliphate and returning Egypt to the Sunni Abbasid caliph. After Nur al-Din died in 1174, Saladin peacefully entered Damascus, took Hama and Homs, defeated the Zengids at the Battle of the Horns of Hama in 1175 and was proclaimed Sultan of Egypt and Syria by the Abbasid caliph. By 1182 he had taken Aleppo, though he failed to take Mosul, and he escaped two attempts on his life by the Order of Assassins.

On 25 November, at Montgisard near Ramla, a small Templar force surprised his army and he fled to Egypt. His army defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, and Jerusalem capitulated on 2 October 1187. Balian of Ibelin threatened to kill the Muslim hostages and destroy the Dome of the Rock if quarter were refused, and Saladin accepted terms allowing ransom. About 18,000 poorer citizens were ransomed through a collection, while another 15,000 were enslaved.

Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem prompted the Third Crusade (1189 to 1192), partly financed by a special Saladin tithe in 1188. Saladin died of a fever at Damascus on 4 March 1193, having given away most of his wealth; he was buried in a mausoleum beside the Umayyad Mosque. Medieval Europeans held him up as a model of kingship, and Dante placed him among the virtuous non-Christians in limbo. His reputation had been largely forgotten in the Muslim world, eclipsed by figures such as Baybars, until the 19th century, when Walter Scott's romantic portrayal and Wilhelm II's visit to his tomb in 1898 helped to make him a hero of the struggle against the West in the Arab world.
salamanca: Salamanca lies on the northern half of the Meseta Central, in the west-central part of the Iberian Peninsula, straddling the Tormes river, in the comarca of Campo Charro. It is the capital of the Province of Salamanca and stands 64 kilometres from Zamora, 121 kilometres from Valladolid and 123 kilometres from Portugal. The three small hills on which settlements grew, formed by the erosion of two streams, and the nearness of the river suited the early functions of defence and control of the surrounding land.

The Iron Age hilltop site of Cerro de San Vicente, on the right bank of the Tormes, is the first stable settlement, dating to the 7th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE a settlement at the Teso de las Catedrales had consolidated under the influence of the Vaccaei and Vettones, Celtic tribes. After Roman conquest it became the civitas of Salmantica. After the Roman period the Alans, then the Visigoths, held it, and in 589 it was an episcopal seat that sent bishops to the councils of Toledo. Christian resettlement under the Kingdom of León, led by Raymond of Burgundy, took hold in the 11th century.

Salamanca joined the revolt of the Communities of Castile in 1520 against the taxes of Charles V, and afterwards the king had the upper parts of the towers of the rebels' palaces removed. During the Peninsular War the city was occupied by the troops of Marshal Soult in 1809 and stayed in French hands until the Battle of Arapiles in 1812, when an Anglo-Portuguese army under Wellington defeated Marmont's French army. The French destroyed much of the city for building materials, including the university's colegios mayores.

The University of Salamanca received its royal charter as an Estudio General from Alfonso IX of León in 1218. It was the first institution to receive the title of university, in 1254, and under Alfonso X its schools of canon and civil law drew students even from Paris and Bologna. Antonio de Nebrija's grammar of Spanish appeared here in 1492, and Hernán Cortés studied here briefly before leaving in 1501.

The Old City was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. It holds the Baroque Plaza Mayor, designed by Alberto and Nicolás Churriguera, the Casa de las Conchas, whose facade carries about 350 scallop shells, and two cathedrals, the Romanesque Old Cathedral of the 12th century and the much larger Gothic New Cathedral, begun in the 16th century and completed in the 18th. The city had 144,458 inhabitants in 2024 and its Holy Week processions are of international tourist interest.
salvador-allende: Salvador Guillermo Allende Gossens was born on 26 June 1908 in Santiago. His family belonged to the Chilean upper middle class and had a long tradition of involvement in progressive and liberal causes. His grandfather was a prominent physician and social reformer who founded one of the first secular schools in Chile. Allende was of Basque and Belgian descent. In 1938 he directed the campaign of the Popular Front headed by Pedro Aguirre Cerda, and as Minister of Health in the following government he passed safety laws for factory workers, higher pensions for widows, maternity care and free lunches for schoolchildren.

Allende was a committed member of the Socialist Party, which he helped found, and over nearly forty years was a senator, a deputy and a cabinet minister. He ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 1952, 1958 and 1964. In 1970 he won a close three-way race as the Popular Unity candidate and was confirmed in a run-off by Congress. As president he pursued what he called the Chilean Path to Socialism, representing the more moderate faction of his party, while its left wing under Carlos Altamirano sought a more radical course.

In the first year his economy minister Pedro Vuskovic's policy brought 12% industrial growth, but by 1972 inflation of the escudo reached 140%. His government returned land to the Mapuche and in 1971 re-established relations with Cuba. A 24-day strike began in October 1972, and on 29 June 1973 Colonel Roberto Souper's tank regiment surrounded La Moneda in a failed coup known as the Tanquetazo. On 22 August 1973 the Chamber of Deputies voted 81 to 47 to accuse the government of breaching the Constitution.

In early September 1973 Allende considered resolving the crisis with a plebiscite, to be announced on 11 September. That day the military under Augusto Pinochet staged the coup. As troops surrounded La Moneda he spoke to Chileans on live radio, refused an offer of safe passage and died in his office, by suicide, though the exact circumstances are disputed. The junta that followed dissolved Congress, and at least 3,095 civilians disappeared or were killed. Allende is buried in the general cemetery of Santiago, and many socialists revere him as a hero and martyr.
salzburg: Salzburg stands on both banks of the River Salzach at the northern edge of the Alps. The mountains lie to the south and rolling plains to the north; the nearest alpine peak, the Untersberg at 1,972 metres, is less than 16 kilometres from the centre. The old town is flanked by two smaller hills, the Mönchsberg and the Kapuzinerberg, and dominated by the Hohensalzburg Fortress. The city lies about 150 kilometres east of Munich and 300 kilometres west of Vienna.

The area has been inhabited continuously since the Neolithic. In the La Tène period it was an administrative centre of the Celtic Taurisci in the Kingdom of Noricum. After the Roman invasion of 15 BCE the settlements on the surrounding hills were abandoned for a Roman city, which received the status of a municipium in 45 CE and became one of the most important cities of the province of Noricum.

When Noricum collapsed in 488, part of the Romano-Celtic population remained, and in the sixth century it came under the Baiuvarii. The Life of Saint Rupert credits Rupert with the city's rebirth: Duke Theodo II of Bavaria gave him the remains of the Roman town and an upper castle on the Nonnberg Terrace, and in return he was to evangelise the east and south-east of Bavaria.

Independence from Bavaria was secured in the late fourteenth century, and the archbishopric became a prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire. During the German Peasants' War the archbishop fled to the fortress, which was besieged for three months in 1525. On 31 October 1731 Archbishop Count Leopold Anton von Firmian signed an Edict of Expulsion ordering all Protestant citizens to recant; 21,475 citizens refused and were expelled, and most of them accepted an offer from King Friedrich Wilhelm I of Prussia to settle in East Prussia. Napoleon secularised the archbishopric in 1803. Salzburg passed to Austria in 1805, to Bavaria in 1809 and finally back to Austria under the Treaty of Munich of 1816.

Salzburg's historic centre was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 and is one of the best-preserved city centres north of the Alps. Prince-Archbishop Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau began to rebuild the medieval town on late Renaissance lines, and Santino Solari's cathedral was the first early Baroque church in the city. The Franziskanerkirche dates from 1208, and the Großes Festspielhaus, opened in 1960, was built for the annual Salzburg Festival. The city has three universities, among them the Mozarteum University for music and drama.
samarkand: Samarkand is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia and prospered from its place on the trade route between China, Persia and Europe. There is no direct evidence of when it was founded; researchers at the Institute of Archaeology of Samarkand date it to around 700 BCE. It was the central city of the Sogdian civilisation. It was known as Marakanda when Alexander the Great conquered it in 329 BCE. According to some sources the present name comes from the Sogdian samar, stone, and kand, fort or town, though this cannot be proven.

The Persian Sasanians conquered Samarkand around 260 CE, and under their rule the region became an essential site for Manichaeism. Nomadic Xionites took it between 350 and 375, and the Hephthalites controlled it until the Göktürks, allied with the Sasanians, won it around 560. The armies of the Umayyad Caliphate under Qutayba ibn Muslim captured the city around 712. It was the capital of the Samanid Empire in the 9th century, when New Persian gradually replaced Sogdian, and from 1040 to 1212 it was the capital of the Western Qarakhanid Khaganate.

The Mongols under Genghis Khan conquered the city in 1220. According to the historian Juvayni, Genghis killed all who had taken refuge in the citadel and the mosque, pillaged the city completely and conscripted 30,000 young men and 30,000 craftsmen. Samarkand remained in the Chagatai Khanate until 1370. Timur ruled from 1370 to 1405 and made it the capital of the Timurid Empire. Between 1417 and 1420 his grandson Ulugh Beg built a madrasah that became the first building of the Registan ensemble, and in 1428 he built an observatory whose chief instrument was a wall quadrant with a radius of 40 metres.

Muhammad Shaybani of the Uzbek Shaybanid dynasty took the city in 1501, and it became the capital of the new Bukhara Khanate. Russian forces under General Konstantin Petrovich von Kaufman took the citadel in 1868, and the Russian section of the city was built to the west of the old city. Samarkand was the first capital of the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, from 1925 to 1930.

Samarkand is the second-largest city of Uzbekistan and capital of the Samarkand Region. The Timurid and Uzbek Khanate periods gave it the Registan Square, the Gur-i Amir Mausoleum, the Bibi-Khanym Mosque and the Shah-i-Zinda Necropolis, known for their tilework in cobalt and turquoise. UNESCO added the city to its World Heritage List in 2001 as Samarkand, Crossroads of Cultures.
samnite-wars: The Samnites were a confederation of four tribes living in the mountains east of Campania. Rome and the Samnites made a treaty in 354 BCE whose terms are not recorded; modern historians have proposed that it made the River Liris the boundary between their spheres. Livy, the only continuous source for the first war, says it began when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini and then the Campanians, and Capua surrendered itself to Rome. Modern historians doubt his three Roman victories of 343 BCE. The war ended in 341 BCE in a negotiated peace: Rome accepted that the Sidicini lay in the Samnite sphere but kept its alliance with the Campanians.

The second war grew out of Roman moves in Campania: a colony founded at Fregellae in 328 BCE and the taking of Naples in 326 BCE. In 321 BCE the consuls Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius Albinus were trapped by the Samnite commander Gaius Pontius in the Caudine Forks and surrendered; their soldiers passed unarmed under the yoke and six hundred equites were given as hostages. Livy says Rome rejected the agreement and avenged it, a claim some modern scholars doubt. Fighting resumed in 316 BCE, and in 304 BCE, after the fall of Bovianum, the Samnites sought peace; Livy says the old treaty was restored.

The third war began in 298 BCE, when the Lucanians asked for Roman protection against Samnite invasion. In 295 BCE Rome faced a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senone Gauls. At Sentinum the consul Publius Decius Mus devoted himself, charging into the enemy line to his death, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus won the battle; Livy gives 8,700 Roman dead and 20,000 of the enemy. Livy's surviving narrative ends in 293 BCE, and the last campaigns to 290 BCE are known only in outline.

The Samnites were forced to become allies of Rome, on terms that must have been unequal, and a colony was planted at Venusia in south-eastern Samnia. Gaius Pontius was captured, paraded in a triumph and beheaded. Around Samnia Rome had already bound the Marsi, Marrucini, Paeligni and Frentani by alliance in 304 BCE and the Vestini in 302 BCE, and it annexed the Hernici and the Sabines by giving them citizenship without the vote. The allies supplied soldiers at their own expense and shared the spoils, which greatly enlarged the manpower Rome could call on.
samsung: According to its founder, the name Samsung means three stars: the three stands for something big, numerous and powerful, and the stars for something everlasting. In 1938, in the Japanese era, Lee Byung-chul, a member of a large landowning family, moved to nearby Taikyu and founded the Mitsuboshi Trading Company, in Korean Samsung Sanghoe. It began as a small trading company of forty employees, dealing in dried fish, locally grown groceries and noodles. It prospered, and Lee moved its head office to Seoul in 1947. When the Korean War broke out he was forced to leave Seoul and started a sugar refinery in Pusan named Cheil Jedang.

In 1954 Lee founded the textiles company Cheil Mojik and built its first plant in Taegu, the largest woollen mill in the country at the time. Over the next decades the group diversified into food processing, textiles, insurance, securities and retail. It entered the electronics industry in the late 1960s, and the construction and shipbuilding sectors in the mid-1970s. In 1980 it acquired Hanguk Jeonja Tongsin, based in Kumi, and entered telecommunications hardware, with switchboards as its early products; in the 1980s the company grouped its electronics under Samsung Electronics. After Lee died in 1987 the group was divided into five business groups: Samsung Group, Shinsegae Group, CJ Group, Hansol Group and JoongAng Group.

Samsung Group is a South Korean conglomerate headquartered in Samsung Town in Seoul. It is a chaebol, a family-controlled conglomerate, and comprises around 80 companies in fields such as construction, consumer electronics, financial services, shipbuilding and medical services. Key affiliates include Samsung Electronics, Samsung Heavy Industries, Samsung Engineering, Samsung C&T Corporation and Samsung Life Insurance. The group has had a powerful influence on South Korea's economic development, politics, media and culture, and has been a major driving force behind the Miracle on the Han River. Its logo is blue, said to symbolise stability, reliability and corporate social responsibility. The smartphone platform was launched with the Samsung Solstice line in 2008, later developed into the Galaxy line.
samuel-johnson: Samuel Johnson was born on 18 September 1709 in Lichfield, Staffordshire, above the bookshop of his father Michael Johnson. His mother Sarah was 40, an unusually late age for a first birth, and the infant did not cry, so the family feared for his life and had him baptised at once. He attended Pembroke College, Oxford, until lack of money forced him to leave. His father fell deeply into debt and died in December 1731, when Johnson was twenty-two. Johnson was turned down for a post as usher at Stourbridge Grammar School because he had no degree. After working as a teacher he moved to London and began writing for The Gentleman's Magazine.

His early works include the poem London (1738), the Life of Mr Richard Savage (1744) and the poem The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749). In 1746 a group of publishers approached him to make an authoritative dictionary, and a contract with William Strahan and associates, worth 1,500 guineas, was signed on 18 June. Johnson said the work would take three years, remarking that the Académie Française had used forty scholars for forty years. A Dictionary of the English Language appeared in 1755. Critics included Thomas Babington Macaulay, who called Johnson a wretched etymologist, while the biographer Walter Jackson Bate called it one of the most notable single achievements of scholarship.

Johnson then wrote the novella The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759) and edited The Plays of William Shakespeare (1765). In 1763 he befriended James Boswell, and in August 1773 the two set out on a journey to Scotland, which Johnson described in A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland (1775). There he entered the dispute over James Macpherson's Ossian poems, arguing that they could not be translations of ancient Gaelic writing because nothing had been written in that language in those times. Near the end of his life he wrote Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets (1779–1781), biographies and critical appraisals of 52 poets.

Johnson suffered from scrofula, gout, deafness in one ear and blindness in one eye, and from long periods of depression. His tics and gestures, closely recorded by Boswell, have led to a posthumous diagnosis of Tourette syndrome. He died on the evening of 13 December 1784, aged 75, and is buried in Westminster Abbey. In his criticism he preferred contemporary language and was suspicious of Milton's blank verse and obscure allusions. His Dictionary was pre-eminent until the Oxford English Dictionary appeared some 150 years later, and he changed the course of biography; Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson (1791) is described by Bate as the best-known single work of biographical art in the whole of literature.
samurai: Until the late 8th century Japan had a national conscript army, which the imperial court dismantled, ending it by 792. Conscripts were seen as unreliable, and in the war against the Emishi, who relied on mounted warriors, professional mounted archers from wealthy families decided most battles. The government recruited men who already had those skills, acquired through private training funded by their families. The word samurai is thought to come from saburau, to serve, and so means a retainer or vassal; the proper term for a professional warrior is bushi, and the daimyo and the shogun were bushi but were not called samurai.

The Minamoto and Taira clans, both with court positions, became rivals. Taira no Kiyomori became the first bushi given a senior court rank, as chief minister in 1167. After the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled through a military government in Kamakura and was appointed shogun, and in 1192 he created the gokenin class of warrior vassals, who owed the shogun military service in exchange for privileges. The Ōnin War, which began in 1467, brought down the Ashikaga shogunate and led to the Sengoku period, in which daimyo fought each other.

After the Battle of Sekigahara Tokugawa Ieyasu was declared shogun in 1603, and after the siege of Osaka in 1615 there was a period of peace for 250 years. Under the Tokugawa the samurai first became a truly hereditary class, a process begun by Hideyoshi with the Sword Hunt of 1588 and the Separation Edict of 1591. With no warfare they gradually lost their military function; many served as officials, police, teachers or domain administrators, while keeping stipends and the right to bear arms.

After the Meiji Restoration the abolition of the domains, conscription, the ending of hereditary stipends and the removal of privileges such as wearing swords dismantled the basis of samurai status. Former feudal lords became kazoku, nobility, and most former warriors became shizoku, classes that remained legally recognised until 1947.

The samurai class was highly stratified, by the rank of one's lord and the size of one's stipend. Below the daimyo came the hatamoto, who had the right of audience with the shogun, and then the gokenin. Samurai trained from a young age in swordsmanship, archery and horsemanship. Confucianism, Buddhism and, to a lesser extent, Shinto influenced their culture, and the works Hagakure and Gorin no Sho, written in the Edo period, contributed to the development of bushidō.
san-antonio: San Antonio lies in the southern part of Texas, on the Balcones Escarpment at about 202 m above sea level, with the Texas Hill Country reaching into its far north. It is roughly 75 miles south-west of Austin and 150 miles north of the Mexican border. Its gently rolling terrain is dotted with oak trees, mesquite and cacti, and its climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot summers and mild winters. It is the county seat of Bexar County.

When the Spanish arrived, the Payaya people lived near the San Antonio River valley in the San Pedro Springs area and called it Yanaguana, meaning refreshing waters. On 13 June 1691, the feast day of Saint Anthony of Padua, Spanish explorers and missionaries came upon the river and the Payaya settlement and named the place and the river San Antonio in his honour. A Spanish mission and colonial outpost was founded there in 1718, and in 1731 San Antonio became the first chartered civil settlement in present-day Texas.

The city belonged to the Spanish Empire until 1821, to the Mexican Republic from 1821 to 1836, and to the Republic of Texas from 1836 until annexation by the United States, of which it was part from 1846. It was in the Confederate States from 1861 to 1865. The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of San Antonio traces its origin to 27 August 1784 and was raised to an archdiocese in 1926. The San Antonio Express-News has served the area since 1865. The city is a key military centre, with Fort Sam Houston and nearby Lackland and Randolph Air Force Bases.

San Antonio had 1,434,625 residents at the 2020 census and is the second most populous city in Texas after Houston. Five 18th-century Spanish frontier missions, among them the Alamo and those in San Antonio Missions National Historical Park, were designated UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2015. Because of the Alamo Mission the city is often called Alamo City. About 64% of its residents identify as Hispanic, and Roman Catholicism is the largest religious group, a legacy in part of its Spanish and Mexican heritage.
san-diego: San Diego is a city on the Pacific coast of Southern California, next to the Mexican border. Its bay is the surface expression of a north-south nested graben, and the Rose Canyon and Point Loma fault zones are part of the San Andreas Fault system. About 40 miles east of the bay are the Laguna Mountains. The city is known for a mild Mediterranean climate, beaches and parks, and its long association with the United States Navy.

The area is historically home to the Kumeyaay people, whose town on the site was called Kosa'aay, "drying out place". The San Dieguito complex was established in the area at least 9,000 years ago, and the Kumeyaay may have developed from it or arrived around 1000 CE, a question on which scholars differ. The first European to visit was Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo, who claimed the bay for the Spanish Empire in 1542 and named it San Miguel. In November 1602 Sebastián Vizcaíno surveyed the harbour, Mission Bay and Point Loma, and named the area San Diego de Alcalá after Saint Didacus.
The Presidio and Mission San Diego de Alcalá, founded in 1769, formed the first European settlement in what is now California, and the city has been called the Birthplace of California.

In 1821 Mexico won its independence from Spain, and San Diego became part of the Mexican territory of Alta California. The fort on Presidio Hill was gradually abandoned and the town grew on the level land below it. The Mexican government secularized the mission in 1834 and granted most of its lands to former soldiers. The 432 residents of the town petitioned to form a pueblo, and Juan María Osuna was elected its first alcalde.

California was ceded to the United States in 1848 after the Mexican-American War and admitted as a state in 1850. That year San Diego was made the seat of the new County of San Diego and incorporated as a city, with Joshua H. Bean, the last alcalde, as first mayor. Two years later it was bankrupt, and the legislature revoked its charter and placed it under a board of trustees until 1889.

San Diego is the seat of San Diego County and the second most populous city in California, with over 1.4 million residents. Its economy rests largely on military and defence activities, tourism, international trade, research and manufacturing. The San Ysidro Port of Entry connects it with Tijuana, and the city's present charter was adopted in 1931.
san-francisco: San Francisco lies on the West Coast of the United States, at the north end of the San Francisco Peninsula, and its boundaries take in stretches of the Pacific Ocean and San Francisco Bay. Alcatraz, Treasure Island and the adjacent Yerba Buena Island belong to the city, as do the uninhabited Farallon Islands, 43 kilometres offshore. The mainland within the city limits forms roughly what residents call the seven-by-seven-mile square, and the total area, including water, is nearly 600 square kilometres.

The name, Spanish for 'Saint Francis', comes from Mission San Francisco de Asís, founded in 1776 under Padre Francisco Palóu and named for Francis of Assisi. The first civilian pueblo was called Yerba Buena, 'good herb', and the city has officially been San Francisco since 1847, when its alcalde, Washington Allon Bartlett, renamed it.

The earliest evidence of human habitation dates to 3000 BCE. The Ohlone name for the place was Ahwaste, 'place at the bay', and the Yelamu group of the Ramaytush people lived in small villages there. The Portolá expedition, led by Gaspar de Portolá and Juan Crespí, reached the bay on 2 November 1769, the first documented European visit, and noted the strategic value of its large natural harbour. Settlers from New Spain founded the Presidio of San Francisco at the Golden Gate and the Mission San Francisco de Asís on 29 June 1776. The Mission system marked the beginning of the assimilation of the Ramaytush and the decline of their language and culture.

The California gold rush of 1849 brought rapid growth and made San Francisco the largest city on the West Coast. In 1856 it became a consolidated city-county. The earthquake and fire of 1906 destroyed three-quarters of the city, which was quickly rebuilt and hosted the Panama–Pacific International Exposition nine years later. In the Second World War it was a major port of embarkation for naval personnel bound for the Pacific. After the war returning servicemen, immigration, liberalizing attitudes, the beatnik and hippie countercultures and opposition to the Vietnam War led to the Summer of Love and the gay rights movement, which made the city a centre of liberal activism.

San Francisco is a city on the Pacific coast of California whose boundaries are the same as those of its county; the 2020 census counted 873,965 people. It is known for its steep hills, Chinatown and the Mission District, and for landmarks including the Golden Gate Bridge, cable cars and Alcatraz. The Presidio, the former Spanish military base, is now one of the city's largest parks and the site of museums and institutions.
san-jose-california: San Jose lies in the Santa Clara Valley, in the southern part of the San Francisco Bay Area, and is the county seat of Santa Clara County. Its northernmost part touches San Francisco Bay at Alviso. The Guadalupe River runs north from the Santa Cruz Mountains through the city. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm, dry summers and cool, wet winters. The city takes its name from the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe, its predecessor.

The Tamien nation of the Ohlone people has lived in San Jose and most of the Santa Clara Valley since around 4,000 BCE. California was claimed for the Spanish Empire in 1542, but for nearly 200 years it remained a distant frontier largely controlled by the Native nations. British gains after the Treaty of Paris of 1763 and Russian colonisation in the north-west led the Spanish authorities to sponsor the Portolá Expedition of 1769. San Jose was founded on 29 November 1777 as the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe, the first city founded in the Californias.

It became part of the First Mexican Empire in 1821, and in 1833 Mexico secularised the California missions. The United States completed its conquest of California by the end of 1847, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 formally ceded it. On 15 December 1849 San Jose became capital of the territory of California, and on California's admission to the Union on 9 September 1850 it became the state's first capital.

After the Second World War the city grew rapidly: under the City Manager Dutch Hamann, in office from 1950 to 1969, it annexed property 1,389 times and grew from 17 to 149 square miles. The nickname Silicon Valley was coined in 1971, and in 1988 Mayor Tom McEnery adopted the motto Capital of Silicon Valley. The 1990 census showed that San Jose had surpassed San Francisco in population.

San Jose is the most populous city in the San Francisco Bay Area and in Northern California, with 1,013,240 residents at the 2020 census. San José State University, founded in 1862 as the California State Normal School, has been in downtown San Jose since 1870. The city has historic ethnic districts such as Japantown and Little Portugal, a large Vietnamese population and the largest Sikh gurdwara outside India. Alum Rock Park, established in 1872, is the oldest municipal park in California.
san-jose-costa-rica: San José stands in the middle of Costa Rica, in the mid-west of the Central Valley. It is the seat of national government, the focus of political and economic activity and the country's chief transport hub. Together with the neighbouring cantons of Alajuela, Heredia and Cartago it forms the Greater Metropolitan Area. The city is named in honour of Joseph of Nazareth. Its climate is tropical wet and dry, with average temperatures that vary little through the year.

San José was founded in 1736 by order of the Cabildo de León, to gather the scattered inhabitants of the Aserrí Valley. A chapel was completed a year later with help from the church of Cartago, and St Joseph was chosen as parish patron, which gave the town its name. Unlike Cartago, it was not founded by formal decree and so lacked a city government until the Constitution of Cádiz was enacted in 1812. On 18 October 1813 the presbyter Florencio del Castillo defined it as a city, but the title was lost in 1814 when Ferdinand VII annulled the proceedings of the courts. It was restored in 1820, and in 1823 San José became the capital of Costa Rica.

The installation of the Tobacco Factory in 1782 spurred growth, and capital from tobacco plantations let the city surpass neighbouring provinces economically. In the late 19th century the French coffee entrepreneur Monsieur Amon created the first modern urban neighbourhood, Barrio Amon, in Belle Époque style; it and the National Theater remain symbols of the Costa Rican coffee golden age. The University of Santo Tomas, the country's first university, was established in San José in 1843 and closed in 1888.

San José is the capital and largest city of Costa Rica, with an estimated 352,381 people in its canton in 2022. It holds the National Museum of Costa Rica and the National Theater, considered the finest historic building in the capital; El Teatro Variedades, built in 1892, is its oldest theatre. The Museum of Pre-Columbian Gold and the Museum of Jade are also in the city. The University for Peace, established by the United Nations General Assembly in 1980, is located in San José.
san-juan-puerto-rico: San Juan lies on the north-eastern coast of Puerto Rico in the Northern Plains region, facing the Atlantic Ocean. The municipality covers 199.2 square kilometres, of which about a third is water. Its main bodies of water are San Juan Bay and two natural lagoons, the Condado and San José. The old city stands on the Islet of San Juan, and all the city's beaches face the Atlantic.

The Taíno were the original inhabitants before Europeans reached the island in 1493. The site of San Juan marked the boundary between two Taíno territories, Guaynabo and Haimanio, led by the chiefs Mabo and Yuisa. In 1508 Juan Ponce de León founded the settlement of Caparra, named for a Roman town in the Spanish province of Cáceres, the birthplace of Nicolás de Ovando, then governor of Spain's Caribbean territories. The settlement was later moved to a site then called Puerto Rico, Spanish for rich port.

San Juan was the first stopover in the Americas for ships sailing from Spain. A network of fortifications was built to protect the transports of gold and silver from the New World to Europe, and the rich cargoes made the port a target of foreign powers. The Puerta de San Juan, built in 1635, is the main preserved gate of the colonial walls.

On 8 May 1898 United States Navy ships under Rear Admiral William T. Sampson arrived at San Juan Bay during the Spanish–American War. On 10 May Captain Ángel Rivero Méndez, commanding the Spanish forces in the fortress of San Cristóbal, ordered his men to fire on USS Yale, the first attack against the Americans on the island.

San Juan is the capital and most populous municipality of Puerto Rico, an unincorporated territory of the United States. It is the second oldest European-established capital in the Americas, after Santo Domingo. The historic district of Old San Juan, with the former defensive walls, Fort San Felipe del Morro, Fort San Cristóbal and La Fortaleza, the oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the Americas, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
san-salvador: San Salvador lies in the Salvadoran highlands at an average height of 658 metres, surrounded by volcanoes. The Boquerón Volcano rises to 1,893 metres above the metropolitan area. The city has a tropical wet and dry climate, with a dry season from November to April and a rainy season from May to October, when thunderstorms come almost daily.

The conquistador Gonzalo de Alvarado founded a mission he named San Salvador in 1525. The name probably refers to the feast of the Transfiguration, called Divino Salvador in Spanish, held on 6 August, the day on which in 1456 Pope Callixtus III commemorated the Christian victory at the Siege of Belgrade. Names such as San Salvador became a popular choice for churches and places, and Christopher Columbus had given it to the island of Guanahani in 1492. The city was part of the Kingdom of Spain until 1821, and then of the Mexican Empire in 1822 and 1823 and of Central America until 1841.

The city has suffered from many severe earthquakes, of which the most disastrous came in 1854. When the San Salvador volcano erupted in 1917, three major earthquakes damaged the city so badly that the government temporarily moved the capital to Santa Tecla. On 10 October 1986 another earthquake killed between 1,000 and 1,500 people and left 200,000 homeless. Colonial buildings, cathedrals above all, have been destroyed over time, and the few notable buildings of the historic downtown that survive date from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

San Salvador is the capital and largest city of El Salvador, with 525,990 inhabitants in the municipality. It is the seat of the Legislative Assembly and the Supreme Court. The National Theatre, built in 1917, is the oldest theatre in Central America, and the National Palace dates from 1905.
sanaa: Sanaa stands at about 2,300 metres above sea level, on a plain of the same name, the Haql Sanaa, between the mountains of Jabal An-Nabi Shu'ayb and Jabal Tiyal. The plain is roughly 50 to 60 km long from north to south and about 25 km wide, bordered by cliffs and mountains from which wadis descend. The Old City is known for its tower houses of stone and fired brick, which can rise to eight storeys. Their ground floors were traditionally used for grain and animals, and the top room, the mafraj, serves as a second reception room.

The city was a secondary capital of the Kingdom of Saba, whose main capital was the oasis of Marib. Its name is probably derived from a Sabaic root meaning well-fortified. From the time of Muhammad, around 622 CE, Sanaa was the governing seat of Yemen until independent sub-states appeared, and all of Yemen's states competed to control it.

The Ottoman Empire entered Yemen in 1538, under Suleiman, and conquered Sanaa in 1547 under Özdemir Pasha. In 1602 the local Zaydi imams, led by Imam al-Mu'ayyad, reasserted their control, and Ottoman troops were forced out in 1629. In 1904, as Ottoman influence waned, Imam Yahya took power in Sanaa and followed a policy of isolation that left the city with little new infrastructure. Before the revolution of 1962 society was divided into five ranked groups, headed by the sayyids and the qadis. The Jewish community, present in Yemen since the 5th century BCE, was expelled in 1679 and returned in 1680 to a quarter outside the walls. After 1948 about 49,000 of an estimated 51,000 Yemenite Jews were airlifted to Israel.

Sanaa is the capital and largest city of Yemen, with a population of about 3,300,000 in 2023. It grew rapidly from the 1960s, when it became the capital of the republic and a new city spread beyond the old one. The Old City, enclosed by clay walls 9 to 14 metres high and holding more than 100 mosques, 12 hammams and 6,500 houses, was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The Great Mosque is more than 1,400 years old. The sung tradition al-Ghina al-San'ani, which dates to the 14th century, was designated UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2003.
sandro-botticelli: Alessandro di Mariano di Vanni Filipepi, known as Botticelli, was born in Florence in a house on the Borgo Ognissanti and lived in the same area all his life. He was the youngest of the four surviving children of the tanner Mariano di Vanni d'Amedeo Filipepi and his wife Smeralda. His birth date is unknown, but his father's tax returns, which give his age as two in 1447 and thirteen in 1458, show that he was born between 1444 and 1446. Giorgio Vasari reported that Botticelli was first trained as a goldsmith. From about 1461 or 1462 he was apprenticed to Fra Filippo Lippi, from whom he learned intimate compositions with melancholic figures drawn in clear contours.

Botticelli was an independent master throughout the 1470s, and his reputation rose. His only significant time away from Florence was spent painting in Pisa in 1474 and, in 1481 to 1482, in the Sistine Chapel in Rome, where Pope Sixtus IV summoned him and other Florentine and Umbrian painters to fresco the walls. He received patronage from members of the Medici family, including Lorenzo de' Medici and his circle.

The 1480s were his most successful decade. Primavera of about 1482 and The Birth of Venus of about 1485, both now in the Uffizi, depicted classical mythology on a very large scale, which was virtually unprecedented in Western art since antiquity. In the same decade he painted many Madonnas and altarpieces, among them the Bardi Altarpiece, finished by February 1485, and the San Marco Altarpiece, his largest. By the 1490s his style became more personal and to some extent mannered, and his last works moved in a direction opposite to that of Leonardo da Vinci and the painters of the High Renaissance, towards a style many have called more Gothic or archaic.
He painted dozens of Madonnas, many of them in the round tondo shape, as well as portraits, although fewer than have been attributed to him. He had a lifelong interest in Dante.

According to Vasari, Botticelli became a follower of the Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola, who preached in Florence from 1490 until his execution in 1498, gave up painting and fell into poverty. Botticelli died on 17 May 1510 and was buried in the church of Ognissanti. His reputation was then eclipsed longer than that of any other major European artist, until the Pre-Raphaelites rediscovered him in the late 19th century.
sandzak: Sandžak covers around 8,500 square kilometres between the south-eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the borders with Kosovo and Albania. Six of its municipalities are in Serbia (Novi Pazar, Sjenica, Tutin, Prijepolje, Nova Varoš and Priboj) and seven in Montenegro (Pljevlja, Bijelo Polje, Berane, Petnjica, Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav). The name is the Serbo-Croatian form of the Ottoman Turkish sancak, a province; Serbs have historically known the region as Raška, of which it was part in the 12th century.

The Ottoman Empire invaded the Serbian Despotate in 1455. The spread of Islam in Sandžak had several causes: Muslims did not pay the jizya tax or the child levy and were privileged over Christians in administration and the courts; after the Great Turkish War (1683–1699) part of the Orthodox population was driven north and the land was settled by people who were or became Muslim; and the region was a centre of trade. Until 1790 it belonged to the Sanjak of Bosnia, which is why its Muslims identify with the Slavic Muslims of Bosnia.

When Serbian and Montenegrin troops seized the region in October 1912, many Slavic Muslims and Albanians left for Ottoman Turkey. In 1919 an Albanian revolt in the Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav districts against inclusion in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was put down; seven hundred Albanians were killed in Rožaje and about 450 civilians in Plav and Gusinje.

In 1941 the region was partitioned between Italian-held Montenegro, the Italian protectorate of Albania and German-occupied Serbia, and Muslim militias, Chetniks and Partisans fought there. On 2 March 1942 the Jews of Novi Pazar were rounded up and killed in camps. In May 1943 Chetnik forces under Pavle Đurišić massacred an estimated 5,400 Albanian men, women and children in Bihor, and an estimated 9,000 Muslims in all were killed by Chetniks and affiliated groups during the war. A Partisan council for Sandžak, founded at Pljevlja on 20 November 1943, accepted on 29 March 1945 the division of the region along the line of 1912.

The municipalities of Sandžak have around 361,656 inhabitants. Bosniaks form 54.8 per cent, Serbs 30 per cent, Montenegrins 5 per cent, people who declare themselves Muslims by ethnicity 3.4 per cent and Albanians 1 per cent. Novi Pazar is the economic and cultural centre. A referendum on autonomy organised by the Muslim National Council of Sandžak between 25 and 27 October 1991 was declared illegal by Serbia. The region remains underdeveloped, and census data show emigration by all its peoples.
sanskrit: Sanskrit is a classical language of the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family. It arose in South Asia after its predecessor languages had spread there from the northwest in the late Bronze Age, and it is one of the three earliest documented languages descended from Proto-Indo-European. Its closest ancient relatives are the Nuristani languages of the Hindu Kush and the Iranian languages Avestan and Old Persian.

The oldest form is Vedic Sanskrit, found in the Rigveda, a collection of 1,028 hymns composed between 1500 and 1200 BCE by Indo-Aryan tribes moving east into northwestern India. The Dravidian languages influenced its sounds and syntax. Classical Sanskrit, refined and standardised from the mid-first millennium BCE, was codified in Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī. The epics, the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa, were composed in Epic Sanskrit, used in northern India between 400 BCE and 300 CE.

The word saṃskṛta means well prepared, perfected or polished. The Rigveda was passed on orally by methods of memorisation of exceptional rigour, as a single text with no variant readings, which makes its archaic forms important for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European. Sanskrit has no native script: from around the turn of the first millennium CE it has been written in various Brahmic scripts, most commonly today in Devanagari. The earliest known inscriptions date from the first century BCE.

For nearly 2,000 years Sanskrit was the language of a cultural order that reached across South Asia, Inner Asia and Southeast Asia, and to some extent East Asia. Inscriptions and manuscripts have been found from Nepal and Tibet to Cambodia, Indonesia, Mongolia, Korea and Japan. Classical Sanskrit covers epics, drama, law, grammar, medicine, astronomy and mathematics; the dramatist Kālidāsa wrote in it, and the foundations of modern arithmetic were first described in it. Its surviving manuscripts number over 30 million.

Sanskrit later stopped being learned as a first language and ceased developing as a living one. It remains the sacred language of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions and is used in worship. It is one of the languages of the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India, and the oldest Sanskrit college, the Benares Sanskrit College, was founded in 1791 under East India Company rule.
santa-fe-new-mexico: Santa Fe lies at the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and is the highest state capital in the United States. Its climate is cold semi-arid, with cool, dry winters and hot summers. The name is Spanish for Holy Faith and is a shortened form of the original La Villa Real de la Santa Fe de San Francisco de Asís. The Tewa call the place P'oegeh, water place, a name that predates European colonisation.

The area was originally occupied by Tanoan peoples who lived in Pueblo villages along the Rio Grande. Tewa built a cluster of homes around the site of today's Plaza sometime after 900 CE, but the Pueblo peoples had abandoned the site for at least 200 years by the time the Spanish arrived in the early 17th century. Juan de Oñate led the first Spanish effort to colonise the region in 1598; the Spanish banished him after his rule was judged cruel to the indigenous population.

Santa Fe was founded in 1610 as the capital of Nuevo México, a province of New Spain, and is the oldest state capital in the United States. The Spanish laid it out by the Laws of the Indies of 1573, around a central plaza with the Palace of the Governors on its north side. It prospered on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro and the Santa Fe Trail. In 1846 General Stephen W. Kearny led some 1,700 soldiers into the city, and by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848 the United States gained New Mexico. Santa Fe became the capital of the territory in 1851 and of the state in 1912.

Santa Fe is the fourth most populous city in New Mexico and the county seat of Santa Fe County. It blends indigenous, Spanish and American influences and has been a UNESCO Creative City in Crafts and Folk Art since 2005. The Plaza and the Palace of the Governors remain at its centre, and its adobe-style Pueblo Revival and Territorial Revival architecture is largely preserved. The city has been associated with science since 1943, when it served as the gateway to Los Alamos National Laboratory.
santander-spain: Santander lies on the northern side of the Bay of Santander, facing the Cantabrian Sea, and owes its existence to the excellent harbour of the bay. The earliest settlers probably chose the north side for practical reasons: it is sheltered from the storms of the Bay of Biscay and has a hillside with good visibility for spotting attackers. Little is known of the earliest settlements.

The place is first mentioned in 1068, in a draft document of King Sancho II. According to the account, Alfonso II the Chaste had founded the Abbey of the Holy Bodies in the 9th century, to house the heads of Saint Emeterius and Saint Celedonius. Alfonso VIII of Castile granted a fuero, or charter, in 1187. The shipyards were ordered by the king to take timber from the Cantabrian forests, and the town had to give the monarchy a ship each year. By the end of the 15th century it had about 4,000 or 5,000 inhabitants. It became a city officially in 1755.

On 3 November 1893 the steamship Cabo Machichaco caught fire while being unloaded at a pier. About 40 tonnes of dynamite in her holds exploded, killing about 590 people, injuring about 2,000 and destroying at least 65 buildings near the harbour.

In the Spanish Civil War the Nationalist uprising of 1936 in Santander was defeated, and the city stayed with the Republican government. Nationalist forces captured it in the Battle of Santander on 26 August 1937. Adam Hoschild counts at least 1,267 people executed after quick trials in the weeks that followed. In 1941 a great fire burned for two days, destroyed the greater part of the medieval town centre and gutted the Romanesque cathedral. Only one person died, a firefighter, but thousands of families were left homeless.

Santander is the capital of the autonomous community of Cantabria. The cathedral keeps its lower church, built around 1200 in a style passing from Romanesque to Gothic. The port remains active, with ferry services to the United Kingdom and Ireland, and the bank Banco Santander was founded in the city.
santiago: Santiago lies in the centre of the Santiago Basin, a flat, bowl-shaped valley of fertile land surrounded by mountains. The main chain of the Andes flanks it to the east and the Chilean Coastal Range to the west, with the Cordón de Chacabuco to the north. The basin measures about 80 kilometres north to south and 35 kilometres east to west, and the Mapocho River flows through the city. A few island hills, among them Cerro Santa Lucía, rise from the plain. The historic centre, the Plaza de Armas, lies at 565 metres.

Archaeological evidence suggests that the first human groups reached the basin around the 10th millennium BCE, nomadic hunter-gatherers who travelled from the coast to hunt guanacos during the Andean snowmelt. By around 800 CE the first permanent settlers had established agricultural communities along the Mapocho, growing maize, potatoes and beans. The villages of the Picunche, whom the Incas called the Promaucae, were under Inca rule from the late 15th century to the early 16th, and the Incas placed a settlement of mitimas in the valley.

The conquistador Pedro de Valdivia, sent by Francisco Pizarro from Peru, arrived in the Mapocho valley on 13 December 1540, after a long journey from Cusco. He founded the city as Santiago del Nuevo Extremo on 12 February 1541, naming it for his home region of Extremadura and for James the Great, patron saint of Spain. It was to be the capital of his governorship of Nueva Extremadura.

The city consolidated as the capital of the Captaincy General of Chile despite food shortages, Indigenous attacks, floods and devastating earthquakes, notably in 1647. It remained the political centre during the Chilean War of Independence, which began with the First Government Junta in 1810 and ended in patriot victory at the Battle of Maipú in 1818. The Universidad de Chile traces its roots to 1622, and the 19th century brought railway construction and major educational and cultural institutions.

Santiago is the capital and largest city of Chile, and its metropolitan area holds over a third of the national population. The presidential palace, the Palacio de La Moneda, stands there, while the National Congress meets mainly in nearby Valparaíso. Few colonial buildings survive because earthquakes regularly strike the country, among them the Church of San Francisco of 1586 and the Casa Colorada of 1769. Its cathedral on the Plaza de Armas was built between 1784 and 1805 under the architect Joaquín Toesca.
santiago-de-compostela: Santiago de Compostela lies in the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula, in the province of A Coruña, at an altitude of about 370 metres. Its climate is oceanic, and the Atlantic winds and surrounding mountains give it some of the highest rainfall in Spain. Santiago is the Galician form of the Vulgar Latin Sanctus Iacobus, Saint James. Compostela probably comes from the Latin compositum tella, a well-ordered burial ground, though folk etymology derives it from Campus Stellae, field of the star.

The area was a Roman cemetery by the 4th century and was occupied by the Suebi in the early 5th. In 585 it passed to the Visigothic Kingdom, and around 750 the bishopric of Iria was incorporated into the Kingdom of Asturias. Between 818 and 842, in the reign of Alfonso II of Asturias, Bishop Theodemar of Iria claimed to have found remains attributed to Saint James the Greater. According to a medieval legend, a bright star guided a shepherd, Pelagius the Hermit, to the burial site. A settlement and pilgrimage centre grew around the place and was called Compostella by the 10th century.

After the centre of Asturian power moved from Oviedo to León in 910, several kings of Galicia and León were crowned there, among them Ordoño IV in 958, Bermudo II in 982 and Alfonso VII in 1111, by which time Compostela was the capital of the Kingdom of Galicia. Viking raiders attacked the town in the 10th century, and in 997 Ibn Abi Aamir, known as al-Mansur, assaulted and partly destroyed it but showed no interest in the relics.
