In the 12th century, under Bishop Diego Gelmírez, Compostela became an archbishopric and drew a large multinational population, and its shrine became second only to Rome and Jerusalem among Catholic shrines.

Santiago de Compostela is the capital of the autonomous community of Galicia and has 96,260 inhabitants. Its Old Town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985. The Obradoiro façade of the cathedral is shown on Spanish euro coins of 1, 2 and 5 cents. The University of Santiago de Compostela was established in the early 16th century.
santo-domingo: Santo Domingo lies on the southern coast of the island of Hispaniola, on the Caribbean Sea, at the mouth of the Ozama River, which divides the city into eastern and western sections. The historic Colonial Zone is on the west side. The land is a coastal plain of flat to gently rolling terrain, with some low limestone hills in the surrounding region. The climate is tropical, with trade winds moderating the heat and humidity, and a rainy season from May to November. Its natural harbour has long made it an important port and commercial centre in the Caribbean.

Before Christopher Columbus arrived in 1492, the Taíno people lived on the island, which they called Kiskeya, meaning mother of all lands, and Ayiti, the land of the high mountains. Columbus later named it Hispaniola. The island then consisted of five chiefdoms, Marién, Maguá, Maguana, Jaragua and Higüey, ruled by the caciques Guacanagarix, Guarionex, Caonabo, Bohechío and Cayacoa.

The Spanish Empire founded Santo Domingo in 1496, and it became the first seat of Spanish colonial rule in the New World, the Captaincy General of Santo Domingo. It is the site of the first university, cathedral, castle, monastery and fortress in the Americas. The Universidad Autónoma de Santo Domingo, established in 1538, is the oldest university in the Americas. From 1936 to 1961 the city was called Ciudad Trujillo, after the Dominican dictator Rafael Trujillo, who named the capital after himself. After his assassination it resumed its original name.

Santo Domingo, officially Santo Domingo de Guzmán, is the capital and largest city of the Dominican Republic, with a city population of about one million and a metropolitan area of more than four million. It is coterminous with the Distrito Nacional, and the presidency, ministries, National Congress and Supreme Court of Justice are in the metropolitan area. The Zona Colonial, bordered by the Ozama, has early 16th-century palatial houses and churches in late medieval style, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990. The Church and Convent of los Dominicos is the oldest Catholic building in continuous use in the Americas and was the headquarters of the first university there.
sao-paulo: São Paulo stands on a plateau beyond the Serra do Mar, part of the Brazilian Highlands, at an average elevation of about 799 metres above sea level and only some 70 kilometres from the Atlantic. Two highways, the Anchieta and the Imigrantes, descend the range to the port of Santos. The Tietê River and its tributary the Pinheiros once supplied fresh water and leisure but became heavily polluted by industrial effluent in the later 20th century. The municipality covers 1,521.11 square kilometres.

The oldest archaeological artefacts found in the municipality come from the Morumbi site and are thought to date from about 3500 BCE. In 1532 Martim Afonso de Sousa founded São Vicente, the first Brazilian village, on the coast. The village of São Paulo dos Campos de Piratininga dates from 25 January 1554, when Jesuit priests founded the Colégio de São Paulo de Piratininga to catechise the indigenous peoples. The college of twelve priests included Manuel da Nóbrega and José de Anchieta, and they built a mission on a steep hill between the Anhangabaú and Tamanduateí rivers.

In the colonial period the city was the centre and starting point of the expeditions of the Paulista bandeirantes, settlers who pushed the country's territorial and economic expansion. Its wealth was consolidated in the Brazilian coffee cycle of the mid-19th century. The First and Second World Wars and the Great Depression hit coffee exports and forced rich growers to invest in industry, which drew immigrants, mainly from Italy, and migrants from the north-east. The population grew to 8.5 million inhabitants in 1980.

In 1960 the city passed Rio de Janeiro as the most populous in Brazil. Landmark events of Brazilian history took place there, among them the Cry of Ipiranga, the Modern Art Week, the 1932 Revolution and the Diretas Já movement.

São Paulo is the capital of the state of São Paulo and the largest city in Brazil, with 11,244,369 people at the 2010 census and a metropolitan area of more than 20 million. Portuguese is the main language. The city is known as the most multicultural in Brazil, with the largest Arab, Italian and Japanese communities in the world, and neighbourhoods such as Bixiga, Bom Retiro and Liberdade.
sappho: Little is known for certain about Sappho's life. She came from a wealthy family on the island of Lesbos and lived at the end of the seventh and the beginning of the sixth century BCE, a contemporary, according to most ancient sources, of the poet Alcaeus and the tyrant Pittacus. Her poetry is the only contemporary source for her life, and the earliest surviving biography dates from the late second or early third century CE, some eight centuries after her time.
Ancient authors drew on statements in her poems that they assumed were autobiographical. Tradition gives her three brothers, Charaxos, Larichos and Eurygios. She was exiled to Sicily around 600 BCE.

Sappho probably wrote about 10,000 lines, of which about 650 survive. Only the Ode to Aphrodite is certainly complete. Her poems were written to be sung and were composed in the Aeolic tradition of Lesbos.

She was one of the first Greek poets to adopt the lyric I, speaking from the viewpoint of a specific person. Her poems explore desire, jealousy and love and often the lives of women, and include poems about family, wedding songs and cult hymns. Ancient authors claimed she wrote chiefly love poetry, but papyri published in 2014 contain ten consecutive poems of which only two are certainly love poems.

Scholars have long debated the setting of her poems: teacher, priestess, chorus leader or participant in the symposium have all been proposed. Several prominent classicists have rejected the view of her as a schoolmistress as unsupported by the evidence.

She was among the Nine Lyric Poets esteemed by the scholars of Hellenistic Alexandria, who arranged her poems in at least eight books, grouped by metre. The latest direct copies, on parchment codex pages, date from the sixth and seventh centuries CE, and around the ninth century her poetry seems to have disappeared. The legend that the Church had it burned arose in the Renaissance. In reality it was probably lost because there was too little demand to copy it from papyrus rolls into codices, and because its Aeolic dialect had come to seem provincial.
According to legend she killed herself by leaping from the Leucadian cliffs for love of the ferryman Phaon. The English words sapphic and lesbian derive from her name and that of her island.
sarajevo: Sarajevo lies near the geometric centre of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Sarajevo valley in the middle of the Dinaric Alps, along the Miljacka River, 518 metres above sea level. Forested hills and five major mountains surround it: Treskavica, Bjelašnica, Jahorina, Trebević and Igman. The last four are known as the Olympic Mountains of Sarajevo, because venues for the 1984 Winter Olympics were built on them. The name comes from the Turkish saray, meaning palace or mansion, and scholars disagree on the origin of the ending evo. The official name under Ottoman rule was Saraybosna, the Palace of Bosnia.

One of the earliest settlements in the area is that of the Neolithic Butmir culture, discovered in 1893 at Ilidža by Austro-Hungarian authorities building an agricultural school. The area's flint attracted settlers, and the Butmir people developed distinctive ceramics. The modern city arose in the fifteenth century as an Ottoman stronghold, when the Ottoman Empire extended into Europe. Isa-Beg Ishaković called the town he was going to construct Šeher, Turkish for city. Gazi Husrev-beg established a school of Sufi philosophy in 1537, the first institution that can be classed as tertiary education.

Ottoman rule lasted until 1878 de facto and 1908 de jure, and Austria-Hungary then governed to 1918. Muslims, Orthodox Christians, Roman Catholics and Sephardi Jews shared the city under Ottoman rule while keeping distinct identities, and by 1909 about 50 per cent of its people were Muslim, 25 per cent Catholic, 15 per cent Orthodox and 10 per cent Jewish. In 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a local Young Bosnia activist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, a murder that sparked the First World War. Austro-Hungarian rule ended and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was created.

After the Second World War the city became the capital of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, and grew rapidly. It hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics. During the Bosnian War it endured the longest siege of a capital city in modern history, 1,425 days from April 1992 to February 1996. The 1991 census recorded 527,049 people in the city's ten municipalities, 49.2 per cent of them Bosniaks, 29.8 per cent Serbs and 6.6 per cent Croats. The war displaced hundreds of thousands, most of whom have not returned.

Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the de jure capital of Republika Srpska. All national institutions are there. It is one of the few major European cities with a mosque, a Catholic church, an Orthodox church and a synagogue in the same neighbourhood, and has been called the Jerusalem of Europe. The Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque and the Sarajevo cathedral are among its landmarks.
sardinia: Sardinia is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea after Sicily, with an area of 24,100 square kilometres. It lies 200 kilometres west of the Italian Peninsula, 200 kilometres north of Tunisia and 16.5 kilometres south of Corsica. Its mountains, woods, plains, rocky coasts and sandy beaches have led to its description as a micro-continent. The name is pre-Latin. It appears as ŠRDN on the Phoenician Nora Stone, and some have speculated that the Nuragic Sards were the Sherden, one of the Sea Peoples.

Humans have lived on the island since the end of the Paleolithic, although authors disagree whether the evidence from Corbeddu Cave, about 20,000 years old, is solid or whether occupation is secure only from about 10,000 years ago. The Nuragic civilization flourished from the 18th century BCE to either 238 BCE or, in some parts, the 2nd century CE, and in Barbagia to the 6th century. The Phoenicians began visiting from about the 9th century BCE, using ports such as Caralis, Nora, Bithia, Sulci and Tharros. In the 6th century BCE the Carthaginians planned to annex it, and a first invasion led by Malchus was foiled by Nuragic resistance, but from 510 BCE the southern and west-central part came under Carthaginian rule.

The Vandals conquered the island in 456, and their rule lasted 78 years. In 530 the Vandal governor Godas declared Sardinia independent of Carthage and negotiated with Emperor Justinian I. When Gelimer sent the bulk of his army and navy to subdue him in 533, Justinian's general Belisarius took Carthage, and Sardinia returned to Byzantine rule, which lasted about 300 years apart from a short period after the Ostrogoths invaded in 551.

In 1297 Pope Boniface VIII created a Kingdom of Sardinia and Corsica and offered it to James II of Aragon. Spanish rule followed, and in 1708 the Austrians occupied the island, although in 1717 Cardinal Giulio Alberoni reoccupied it for Philip V of Spain. In 1861 the parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia renamed the state the Kingdom of Italy. Italy became a republic in 1946, and Sardinia has been governed since 1948 under a special statute of autonomy.

Sardinia is one of the twenty regions of Italy and one of five with statutory autonomy. Cagliari is its capital and largest city, followed by Sassari. The Sardinian language and the Algherese dialect of Catalan are recognised as protected minority languages. Thousands of nuraghe, Bronze Age buildings, still characterise the prehistoric landscape, alongside tombs, megalithic circles and well temples, and the Phoenicians and Punics left traces on the coasts.
sarissa: A sarissa had two main parts, a long wooden shaft and a metal tip; some may also have had a metal butt at the other end, with which the weapon could be stood in the ground without damage to the shaft. Ash, which is long, flexible and light, and cornel wood, which is shorter but stronger, are the likeliest woods. It replaced the considerably shorter dory.

Ancient writers agree that its length set it apart, but not on the figure: Theophrastus, a contemporary of Alexander the Great, puts the longest at 12 cubits, and Polybius gives 16 cubits in the original design, reduced in practice to 14. In modern units this suggests about 5.8 m in Alexander's time and perhaps 6.3 m later.

The weapon needed both hands, so the phalangite carried only a smaller shield, the pelta, perhaps hung from a neck strap. On the march the sarissas were held upright; levelled for battle, fully five rows of points projected in front of the first rank, while the rear ranks held theirs angled upward, which also deflected arrows. A phalanx so formed was considered practically invulnerable from the front, but it turned with difficulty, and a soldier out of formation had to fall back on a sword or dagger.

Sarissa-armed phalanxes were vital in the early battles of Alexander, including the Battle of Gaugamela, though in his later campaigns he gradually reduced their importance. The surest way to beat such a phalanx was to break its formation or outflank it, as the Romans did at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. A light cavalry unit of Alexander's army, the sarissophoroi, carried somewhat shorter versions; Nicholas Victor Sekunda argues that the Macedonian cavalry spear is better classed as a xyston.

A leaf-shaped spearhead 51 cm long, found by Manolis Andronikos in a Macedonian tomb at Vergina, shaped much scholarship between 1970 and 2000, but more recent work doubts that it belonged to a sarissa; Sekunda favours a small diamond-shaped iron tip of about 13.5 cm. Earlier estimates put the weight at 5.5 to 6.5 kg, yet Peter Connolly reconstructed a pike 5.8 m long in cherry wood that weighed only 4.05 kg. Scholars also draw on later pikemen, such as the Swiss and the German Landsknecht: preserved English pikes are 5.6 to 5.9 m long, which suggests that the lengths reported for the Macedonian weapon were workable.
saskatchewan: Saskatchewan is bordered by Alberta to the west, the Northwest Territories to the north, Manitoba to the east and Montana and North Dakota to the south. With Alberta it is one of only two landlocked provinces of Canada, and it is the only province without a natural border, since its borders follow the 49th and 60th parallels and the 110th meridian. The overwhelming majority of the population lives in the southern third. The name comes from the Saskatchewan River, which in Cree is kisiskāciwani-sīpiy, swift flowing river.

Indigenous peoples, among them the Cree, Saulteaux, Assiniboine and Sioux, have lived in the region for thousands of years. The first known European to enter it was Henry Kelsey of England in 1690, who travelled up the Saskatchewan River to trade for fur. The first permanent European settlement was the Hudson's Bay Company post at Cumberland House, founded by Samuel Hearne in 1774. Most of the province lay in Rupert's Land, controlled by the Hudson's Bay Company, and in the late 1850s and early 1860s expeditions led by John Palliser and Henry Youle Hind explored the prairie.

Saskatchewan became a province on 1 September 1905, carved out of the North-West Territories. In 1901 there were 19,200 families, and 150,300 only fifteen years later, and women's labour was critical to the survival of family farms and the wheat economy. In the early 20th century the province became a stronghold of Canadian social democracy, and the 1944 provincial election brought North America's first socialist government to office. In 1992 the federal and provincial governments signed a land claim agreement with First Nations in the province.

Regina is the capital and Saskatoon the largest city of Saskatchewan, and roughly half the people live in the two. The economy is based on agriculture, mining and energy. Wheat has long been the best-known crop, and canola production surpassed it in 2017.
saxony: The Free State of Saxony is a landlocked state of Germany. It borders Brandenburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia and Bavaria, and its southern and eastern boundaries form part of Germany's frontiers with the Czech Republic and Poland. The land rises from the lowlands of the North German Plain in the north, which include the Leipzig Bay and much of Lusatia, to uplands along the Czech border.

Some of the largest ancient monumental temples of central Europe stood here, dating from the fifth millennium BCE. Since the late 6th century the area was populated by Polabian Slavs, most prominently the Sorbs, and it was conquered by Francia and organized as the Sorbian March. The territory became part of the Holy Roman Empire by the 10th century, and the Margravate of Meissen was founded in 985 as a frontier march. In 1423 Saxe-Wittenberg became subject to the margravate, ruled by the Wettin dynasty, creating a new and powerful state. Although its centre lay far to the southeast of the old Saxony, it came to be called Upper Saxony and then simply Saxony, while the northern Saxon lands became Lower Saxony.

In 1806 Napoleon made the Electorate of Saxony a kingdom, in exchange for military support. At the Congress of Vienna the king was restored but forced to cede the northern part of the kingdom to Prussia, a loss of nearly 60 percent of the territory and 40 percent of the population. Frederick Augustus III abdicated on 13 November 1918, and Saxony became the Free State of Saxony. It was broken up under communist rule and re-established on 3 October 1990, on German reunification.

Dresden is the capital of Saxony and Leipzig its largest city. Dresden's Baroque cityscape and art collections, Leipzig's musical traditions and the mining heritage of the Ore Mountains are among its best-known cultural features.
saxony-anhalt: Saxony-Anhalt is a landlocked state of Germany of 20,555 square kilometres, bordering Brandenburg, Saxony, Thuringia and Lower Saxony. In the north the North German Plain dominates, with the old Hanseatic towns of Salzwedel, Gardelegen, Stendal and Tangermünde in the sparsely populated Altmark, and the fertile Magdeburg Börde beyond it. The Harz mountains lie in the south-west; their highest peak, the Brocken at 1,141 metres, is the highest in northern Germany. The wine-growing area of Saale-Unstrut lies in the south, and the Halle area forms an agglomeration with Leipzig, known for its chemical industry at Leuna, Schkopau and Bitterfeld.

Saxony-Anhalt has a short history as a state and consists mainly of three historical regions: the area around Magdeburg, the formerly independent Anhalt, and a southern part that had once belonged to Saxony and was annexed by Prussia in the nineteenth century. Anhalt takes its name from Anhalt Castle near Harzgerode. In April 1945 the US Army took control of most of the western and northern area; it withdrew to make way for the Red Army, as the London Protocol of 1944 had agreed. The Soviet administration then merged the Free State of Anhalt, Halle-Merseburg, the governorate of Magdeburg and some further territories with the Province of Saxony, and appointed Erhard Hübener to head the new provincial administration at Halle.

The Province of Saxony was renamed the Province of Saxony-Anhalt on 20 October 1946, and after the Allied decision to dissolve the Free State of Prussia it became the State of Saxony-Anhalt on 6 October 1947. Hübener, elected minister-president in December 1946, was the only governor in the Soviet zone who did not belong to the Socialist Unity Party. The state joined the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 the East German states were dissolved and its territory divided into the districts of Halle and Magdeburg, apart from the area around Torgau, which went to Leipzig. In 1990, during German reunification, the districts were reintegrated as a state, though Torgau did not return and joined Saxony.

Magdeburg is the capital and largest city, and Halle (Saale) the second-largest. The state's constitution was adopted by its Landtag in 1992. Six UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Germany lie in Saxony-Anhalt, among them the Bauhaus sites in Dessau and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, and the Nebra Sky Disc is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Many sites tied to Martin Luther's life stand there, including Lutherstadt Eisleben and Lutherstadt Wittenberg.
scandinavia: The geography of Scandinavia is varied. It includes the Norwegian fjords, the Scandinavian Mountains that cover much of Norway and parts of Sweden, the flat, low land of Denmark, and the archipelagos and lakes of the east. Finland and Sweden have many lakes and moraines, left by the ice age that ended about ten millennia ago. The region extends north of the Arctic Circle but has relatively mild weather for its latitude because of the Gulf Stream.

The name goes back to the Proto-Germanic compound *Skaðin-awjō, which is also the source of Scania, the southernmost province of Sweden. The earliest identified source for Scandinavia is Pliny the Elder's Natural History of the 1st century CE, which describes Scatinavia as an island.

The Viking Age lasted from about 793 to 1066 CE. Scandinavians raided, conquered, colonised and traded across Europe, and their longships took them to North America, where they were the first Europeans to arrive. Those known as Varangians, mostly from what is now Sweden, travelled east along the river routes into Russia. The expansion produced settlements and realms such as the Danelaw, the Kingdom of Dublin, the Duchy of Normandy and the Kievan Rus', and the Faroe Islands, Iceland and Greenland were settled. The North Sea Empire briefly joined large parts of Scandinavia and Great Britain.

Between the 10th and 13th centuries, as the region became Christian and its states formed, petty kingdoms and chiefdoms were unified into Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The historian Sverre Bagge notes that this division suits the geography, since forests, mountains and empty land separated the three.

Later unions followed, notably the Kalmar Union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, which lasted over a century until King Gustav I led Sweden out of it. Denmark and Norway then stayed united until 1814. The Treaty of Kiel of 14 January 1814 dissolved that union and ceded Norway to the King of Sweden, but Norwegian resistance led to a constitution drawn up at Eidsvoll and a personal union with Sweden, which ended in 1905. The Scandinavist movement, which stressed a common heritage, peaked in the middle of the 19th century.

In its narrow, local sense Scandinavia comprises Denmark, Norway and Sweden, a subset of the Nordic countries, which also include Finland and Iceland. In English the word is sometimes used for all of them. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish form a dialect continuum and are considered mutually intelligible. Sámi and Finnish, of the unrelated Uralic family, have also been spoken in the region since prehistory.
schleswig-holstein: Schleswig-Holstein lies at the base of the Jutland Peninsula between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, and covers 15,763 km2. It borders Denmark, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Lower Saxony and Hamburg. The state consists of Holstein, the southern part of the former Duchy of Schleswig, Lauenburg and the formerly independent city of Lübeck. The Kiel Canal connects Brunsbüttel on the North Sea with Kiel on the Baltic Sea.

Saxon Holstein became part of the Holy Roman Empire after Charlemagne's Saxon campaigns in the late 8th century, and from 811 the River Eider was its northern border. Between 500 and 1200 Schleswig was part of Denmark. In the 12th century Duke Abel came into conflict with his brother King Eric IV and won autonomy for Schleswig as a duchy. From 1460 the Danish king ruled both Schleswig and Holstein as their duke, although Holstein belonged to the Holy Roman Empire.

In the 19th century both Danes and Germans claimed the duchies, in a dispute called the Schleswig-Holstein Question. Germans wanted both to join the German Confederation and cited the Treaty of Ribe, by which they were to stay forever undivided, while Danes held that the Eider was Denmark's natural border. Holstein was entirely German-speaking, while Schleswig was predominantly Danish-speaking until a shift to German began in the south in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

In 1848 Denmark tried to annex the area and Prussia invaded, beginning the First Schleswig War, which Denmark won. Prussia and Austria won the Second Schleswig War of 1864, and the territory became the Prussian Province of Schleswig-Holstein rather than the independent state that German Schleswig-Holsteiners had hoped for.

After the First World War the Allies arranged plebiscites in 1920, and the Danish-speaking north returned to Denmark. After the Second World War the province came under British occupation, and on 23 August 1946 the military government reconstituted it as a separate state.

Schleswig-Holstein is the northernmost of the sixteen German states, with its capital at Kiel and other main cities at Lübeck and Flensburg. German is its official language, and Low German, Danish and North Frisian are recognised minority languages. Its culture combines Danish, Frisian and German elements.
schmalkaldic-league: The League was officially established on 27 February 1531 as a defensive religious alliance: its members pledged to defend each other if Emperor Charles V attacked their territories. At the insistence of the Elector of Saxony, membership was conditional on agreement to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession. Unlike earlier alliances such as the League of Torgau it had a substantial military, the members agreeing to provide 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry for their mutual protection.

Its formation, together with the advance of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1532, led Ferdinand of Austria to grant a religious peace, concluded at Nuremberg on 23 July 1532. Supporters of the Reformation obtained religious liberty until the meeting of a council.

In December 1535 the League opened itself to anyone who subscribed to the Augsburg Confession, and Anhalt, Württemberg, Pomerania and the cities of Augsburg, Frankfurt am Main and Kempten joined. It allied with Denmark-Norway in 1538 and gained the Electoral Palatinate in 1545. The members rarely provoked Charles directly, but they confiscated church land, expelled bishops and Catholic princes and helped spread Lutheranism through northern Germany. Martin Luther attended the meeting of 1537, for which he prepared the Smalcald Articles; they were not formally adopted then but entered the Book of Concord in 1580.

For fifteen years the League met no opposition, because Charles was at war with France and the Ottoman Empire. Francis I of France, though he persecuted Protestants at home, supported the princes from 1535 until the Treaty of Crépy in 1544. Once at peace, Charles turned on the League. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 its leaders could not agree on a plan of battle; on 24 April 1547 the imperial forces routed them at the Battle of Mühlberg, and Philip of Hesse surrendered in May. Reformers such as Martin Bucer fled to England.

In 1548 Charles forced the League to accept the Augsburg Interim. A Protestant victory in the Second Schmalkaldic War in 1552 made him flee across the Alps, and Ferdinand signed the Peace of Passau, which granted some freedoms to Protestants. Three years later the Peace of Augsburg gave Lutheranism official status in the Holy Roman Empire and let princes choose the religion of their domains, by the principle of cuius regio, eius religio.
scholar-officials: The Chinese term, shi dafu, joins two ranks that were once distinct. In the order ascribed to the Duke of Zhou under the Western Zhou dynasty, the dafu were aristocrats who served as officers, and the shi stood between them and the ordinary people and could hold only low offices. During the Warring States period, as states annexed one another and bureaucracies grew, talented shi gave valuable service to their lords and gained influence, while dafu became an office and ceased to be a hereditary rank. The two merged. In the scheme of the Four Occupations the scholar-officials stood first, above farmers, artisans and merchants.

From the Han dynasty to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, officials were chosen through the recommendatory and nine-rank systems, and came mostly from prominent clans such as the Wang clan of Langya and the Cui clan of Qinghe, which supplied officials for generations and intermarried with one another and with the imperial family. The civil service examination was officially established in 587 under the Sui dynasty. In the early Tang dynasty Empress Wu Zetian reformed it by instituting a metropolitan examination, whose graduates were called jinshi; candidates were tested on poems and essays.

The Song dynasty is described as the golden age of the class. Examination had become the main path to office and the bureaucracy replaced the aristocracy. The Song was also the only dynasty to grant scholar-officials a judicial privilege: one who committed a crime faced internal impeachment in place of the ordinary courts, and for a lesser offence only a reprimand. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties the fixed form of the eight-legged essay dominated the examinations, and the political climate left officials less free to speak and write. The Qing government abolished the examinations in 1905, and the class gradually disappeared.

Only a few degree-holders became court or local officials. Most stayed in their villages and towns as social leaders: they taught in private schools, organised welfare, helped settle minor disputes, supervised community projects, kept local order, conducted Confucian ceremonies and assisted in collecting taxes. The district magistrate, who was barred from serving in his home district, depended on them for advice, which gave them power to benefit themselves and their clients. In Confucian theory ministers were not mere subordinates and might oppose an unfit ruler. The system offered a path of upward mobility but had no formal safeguard against corruption beyond the moral teaching it examined.
scotland: The mainland of Scotland makes up the northern third of the island of Great Britain, with a total area of 30,977 square miles (80,231 km2). Its only land border, with England, runs for 96 miles (154 km) between the basin of the River Tweed and the Solway Firth. The mainland is divided into the Highlands, a mountainous region in the north and north-west, the Lowlands, a flatter plain across the centre, and the Southern Uplands along the border. Ben Nevis, at 4,413 feet (1,345 m), is the highest peak of the British Isles.

The earliest known evidence of people in Scotland is stone tools of the Hamburgian culture, made by hunter-gatherers who arrived around 14,500 to 14,000 years ago, soon after the ice sheet retreated. Neolithic farmers came about 6000 years ago. Skara Brae on Orkney, the Callanish Stones on Lewis and Maes Howe on Orkney belong to this period, the stone monuments of the third millennium BCE. The Greek sailor Pytheas made the first written reference in 320 BCE, calling the northern tip of Britain Orcas.

The Roman governor Agricola invaded in 79 CE and defeated a Caledonian army at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 83 CE, but within three years the Roman armies had withdrawn to the Southern Uplands. Under Trajan, who reigned from 98 to 117, Roman control had lapsed to the south of a line between the River Tyne and the Solway Firth, where Hadrian later built his wall. The Kingdom of Scotland emerged as a sovereign state in the 9th century and kept its independence from England partly through an alliance with France.

Its extent was largely fixed by the Treaty of York of 1237 with England and the Treaty of Perth of 1266 with Norway. Orkney and Shetland were acquired from Norway in 1472, and Berwick-upon-Tweed was ceded to England in 1482. James VI succeeded to the English and Irish thrones in 1603, and on 1 May 1707 Scotland and England combined as the Kingdom of Great Britain.

Scotland is a country within the United Kingdom, with Edinburgh as its capital and Glasgow as its largest city. The census of 2022 counted 5,436,600 people. A Scottish Parliament was re-established in 1999 with devolved authority over many areas of domestic policy. Scotland keeps its own legal system, education system and religious history. English and Scots are the most widely spoken languages, while Scottish Gaelic is spoken natively mainly in the Hebrides. Its seven World Heritage Sites include St Kilda, the Old Town and New Town of Edinburgh, New Lanark and the Antonine Wall.
screw: Most screws are tightened by clockwise rotation, which is called a right-hand thread. Left-hand threads are used in exceptional cases, such as the left pedal of a bicycle, where the twisting force would tend to loosen a right-hand screw. The head of a screw is usually larger than the body, which gives a bearing surface and stops the screw from being driven deeper than its length. The cylindrical part below the head is the shank, and the distance between threads is the pitch. Screws are normally made from wire in three steps: cold heading, thread rolling and a coating such as zinc to prevent corrosion.

Fasteners such as dowels, pins, wedges, mortises and tenons, dovetails and nails were widespread before the screw. The screw was one of the last of the simple machines to be invented. By the 1st century BCE wooden screws were in common use around the Mediterranean in presses for olive oil and for grape juice. Metal screws used as fasteners were rare in Europe before the 15th century, if known at all, and did not become common until machine tools for mass production developed toward the end of the 18th century. The first documented screwdriver appears in the Housebook of Wolfegg Castle, written between 1475 and 1490, but screwdrivers probably did not become widespread until after 1800.

Standard thread forms came late. The English engineer Sir Joseph Whitworth created the first standard in about 1841, and the British Standard Fine thread was added in 1908 because his thread was too coarse for some uses. The British Association thread was devised in 1884 and standardised in 1903, and its sizes were defined in metric terms. In the United States the Unified Thread Standard is most common, while in much of the world the ISO metric screw thread has displaced the older systems. Whitworth threads are still used in UK scaffolding and on photographic tripods, and BA threads in railway signalling and in clocks and moving-coil meters.
sea-of-azov: The Sea of Azov is a shelf sea about 360 kilometres long and 180 kilometres wide, with an area of 39,000 square kilometres. It joins the Black Sea through the narrow Strait of Kerch, about 4 kilometres wide, and is sometimes regarded as a northern extension of the Black Sea. The Don and Kuban rivers bring sand, silt and shells, which build bays, limans and long narrow spits; the Arabat Spit stretches over 112 kilometres. The inflow keeps the salinity low, almost fresh in places, and the sea is the shallowest in the world, between 0.9 and 14 metres deep. The name Azov probably derives from a settlement whose name comes from the Kipchak Turkish asak or azaq, meaning lowlands.

Traces of Neolithic settlement lie in the area now covered by the sea. In antiquity it was known as the Maeotis Swamp, from the Maeotians who lived by fishing and farming near its northeastern marshes; it remains unclear whether the sea took its name from them or they from it. The marshes around the mouth of the Tanais, today's Don, served as a check on the migration of nomadic peoples from the steppe. Ancient geographers had only a vague idea of its extent: Herodotus judged it as large as the Black Sea, Pseudo-Scylax about half as large, and it was long believed to connect directly with the Arctic Ocean.

The sea was often a theatre of conflict between Russia, seeking naval expansion to the south, and the Ottoman power. In 1695–96 Peter I led two campaigns to take the Turkish fortress of Azov, defended by a garrison of 7,000. The first, in 1695, brought an army of 31 thousand men and 170 cannon to the fortress; after two failed assaults on 5 August and 25 September the siege was lifted. During the Crimean War, British and French forces took Kerch on 12 May 1855 and then besieged Taganrog, which withstood them despite their great superiority in numbers, and their army withdrew around August 1855.

The sea has long been an important waterway, and navigation grew after the Volga–Don Canal was built in 1952, linking it with the Volga. The major ports are Taganrog, Mariupol, Yeysk and Berdyansk. Fishing has long been a major activity, with sturgeon, pike-perch and bream among the valuable species. Dams, over-fishing and pollution have reduced the catch, and the anchovy fisheries have collapsed.
sea-of-japan: The Sea of Japan is almost completely enclosed. The Japanese archipelago separates it from the Pacific Ocean, and like the Mediterranean it has almost no tides. It has a surface area of about 1,050,000 square kilometres, a mean depth of 1,752 metres and a maximum depth of 4,568 metres. It is joined to neighbouring seas by five straits: the Strait of Tartary, La Pérouse Strait, the Tsugaru Strait, the Kanmon Straits and the Korea Strait. All are shallow, which isolates its water and life from the Pacific. The sea has no large islands, bays or capes. Few rivers flow into it, though the four largest rivers of Japan, the Shinano, Ishikari, Agano and Mogami, do.

Its geological history is long. The Japan Sea began to open in the Early Miocene, and the northern and southern parts of the Japanese archipelago separated. The straits formed in recent geological periods, and the Tsugaru and Tsushima straits, the oldest, interrupted the migration of elephants into the Japanese islands about 2.6 million years ago.

For centuries the sea protected Japan from land invasions, particularly by the Mongols. Asian ships had long crossed it, and from the 18th century European ships did too. Russian expeditions of 1733–1743 mapped Sakhalin and the Japanese islands. In the 1780s the Frenchman Jean-François de Galaup, comte de Lapérouse, sailed north across the sea through the strait later named for him. In 1796 the British naval officer William Robert Broughton explored the Strait of Tartary and the coasts of the Russian Far East and the Korean Peninsula. In 1849 the Russian explorer Gennady Nevelskoy found the strait between the mainland and Sakhalin.

American, Canadian and French whaleships hunted in the sea between 1847 and 1892, chiefly for right whales, and then humpbacks. In the peak years of 1848 and 1849 over 170 vessels cruised there in all. The Chinese name for the sea was once the Sea of Whales. Japanese scientific study of the sea began only in 1915 and became systematic from the 1920s.

Several names are in use: Nihonkai in Japan, Donghae, the East Sea, in South Korea, and Yaponskoye more in Russia. Japan holds that the name Sea of Japan has been the internationally accepted term since the early 19th century, while South Korea says that the East Sea was in use before Japanese colonial rule and asks that it be used alongside the other. The International Hydrographic Organization has used the name Japan Sea in its publication on the limits of seas since 1928. Fishing is the dominant economic activity, and Vladivostok, the terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway, is a major port.
sea-of-marmara: The Sea of Marmara lies entirely within Turkey and links the Black Sea and the Aegean Sea by way of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, separating the country's European and Asian sides. It covers 11,350 square kilometres, measures roughly 280 by 80 kilometres, and is considered the smallest sea in the world. Its maximum depth is 1,370 metres. The south coast is heavily indented and has the Gulf of İzmit, the Gulf of Gemlik, the Gulf of Bandırma and the Gulf of Erdek.

The surface water averages about 22 parts per thousand of salt, slightly more than the Black Sea and about two-thirds that of most oceans. At the bottom it is much more saline, averaging about 38 parts per thousand, like the Mediterranean, and this dense water does not rise to the surface.

The sea is named after Marmara Island, the largest island on its south side, which is rich in marble, mármaron in Greek. In classical antiquity it was called the Propontis, from the Greek pro, in front of, and pontos, sea, because the ancient Greeks sailed through it to reach the Black Sea. In Greek mythology a storm on the Propontis brought the Argonauts back to an island they had left, which led to a battle in which either Jason or Heracles killed King Cyzicus, who had mistaken them for his Pelasgian enemies.

Two groups of islands lie in the sea. To the north are the Princes' Islands, made up of the inhabited islands Kınaliada, Burgazada, Heybeliada, Büyükada and Sedef Adası, and several uninhabited ones. They are reached by ferry from both shores of Istanbul and form part of its conurbation. To the south are the Marmara Islands, with Marmara Island, Avşa, Paşalimanı and Ekinlik inhabited and 17 largely uninhabited islands, among them the prison island of Imralı. They lie within Balıkesir Province and are reached from Tekirdağ or from Erdek.

The North Anatolian Fault runs under the sea. It has caused several major earthquakes, among them those of İzmit in August 1999 and Düzce in November 1999. The August earthquake is commonly called the Marmara Earthquake, since its epicentre lay under the sea and the places worst affected, by the shaking and a tsunami, lay along its shores. About one third of Turkey's population lives in the basin, and Istanbul, the largest city of the country, stands on the sea.
second-world-war: The causes of the war included unresolved tensions after the First World War and the rise of fascism in Europe and militarism in Japan. Under the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost around 13 per cent of its home territory and all its overseas possessions, and had reparations imposed and its armed forces limited. Benito Mussolini's fascist movement seized power in Italy between 1922 and 1925, and Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933. Earlier events included Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931, Italy's invasion of Ethiopia from October 1935, the Spanish Civil War, in which Germany and Italy backed General Francisco Franco's Nationalists, and the Second Sino-Japanese War from July 1937.

The war began on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland, and the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany on 3 September. The Soviet Union invaded Poland on 17 September, and the two states partitioned it. In 1940 Germany conquered Norway, Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and France fell in June. In June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In December 1941 Japan attacked American and British territories, including Pearl Harbor, and the United States entered the war. Japan's advance was halted at the Battle of Midway in June 1942.

In early 1943 the Axis were defeated in North Africa and at Stalingrad. In 1944 the Western Allies landed in Normandy while the Soviet Union advanced into Central Europe. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945. The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August, and Japan signed a surrender document on 2 September 1945.

An estimated 60 million to more than 75 million people died, a majority of them civilians. About 6 million Jews were killed in the Holocaust, together with millions of Slavs and over 130,000 Romani. Germany lost a quarter of its pre-war territory and nine million Germans were expelled from the eastern provinces. German and Japanese leaders were tried for war crimes. The United Nations came into being on 24 October 1945, and the Soviet Union and the United States emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the Cold War. The weakened great powers of Europe saw the decolonisation of Africa and Asia follow, and Italy lost its monarchy and colonial empire.
seine: The Seine rises at Source-Seine, about 30 kilometres north-west of Dijon on the Langres plateau, and flows through Paris into the English Channel at Le Havre. Its drainage basin lies in the Paris Basin and covers most of northern France. The river is divided into five parts: the Petite Seine from the sources to Montereau-Fault-Yonne, the Haute Seine to Paris, the Paris waterway, the Basse Seine from Paris to Rouen, and the Seine maritime from Rouen to the sea. Ocean-going vessels can reach Rouen, 120 kilometres from the sea. Because the river is only 24 metres above sea level 446 kilometres from its mouth, it flows slowly and is easily navigated.

The name comes from the Gaulish Sēquana, the Celtic Gallo-Roman goddess of the river, to whom offerings were found at the source. The buried remains of a Gallo-Roman temple lie at the same site, and small statues of the goddess Sequana and other ex-votos found there are now in the Dijon archaeological museum. The source has belonged to the city of Paris since 1864.

On 28 or 29 March 845 an army of Vikings led by a chieftain named Reginherus, possibly another name for Ragnar Lothbrok, sailed up the Seine with siege towers and sacked Paris. On 25 November 885 another Viking expedition, led by Rollo, travelled up the river to attack Paris again. In March 1314 King Philip IV of France had Jacques de Molay, last Grand Master of the Knights Templar, burned on a scaffold on an island in the river in front of Notre Dame de Paris. After the burning of Joan of Arc in 1431 her ashes were thrown into the Seine from the Mathilde Bridge at Rouen, though counter-claims persist without support.

On 9 August 1803 the American engineer Robert Fulton made the first successful test of his steamboat on the Seine beside the Tuileries Garden. The Seine flooded Paris severely in January 1910. In 1944 reaching the Seine was one of the original objectives of Operation Overlord, and the Allies met it within 90 days of D-Day. At the 1900 Summer Olympics the river hosted the rowing, swimming and water polo events.

The Seine is 777 kilometres (483 miles) long, and Paris has 37 bridges across it, among them the Pont Alexandre III and the Pont Neuf. In 1991 UNESCO added the banks of the Seine in Paris to its list of World Heritage Sites. Four large storage reservoirs built since 1950 on the Seine and its tributaries help to keep the river level constant through the city. The river inspired many artists of the 19th and 20th centuries, among them Claude Monet, Camille Pissarro, Georges Seurat and Alfred Sisley.
semitic-languages: The Semitic languages are a branch of the Afroasiatic language family. They occur in written form from a very early date: Akkadian, also known as Assyrian and Babylonian, and Eblaite texts, written in a script adapted from Sumerian cuneiform, appear from about 2600 BCE in Mesopotamia and the north-eastern Levant respectively. Egyptian, from about 3000 BCE, is a sister branch of Afroasiatic, related to Semitic but not part of it. Amorite appeared about 2100 BCE, followed during the 2nd millennium BCE by the Canaanite languages, including Hebrew and Phoenician, by Aramaic, and by Ugaritic. Where Semitic-speaking peoples originated is still debated: Mesopotamia, the Levant, Ethiopia, the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa have all been proposed.

The Semitic languages are notable for their nonconcatenative morphology. Word roots are sets of consonants, usually three, and words are formed by filling in vowels between them. In Arabic the root k-t-b, dealing with writing, gives kitāb, book, and kataba, he wrote; Hebrew uses the same root in katav, he wrote, and michtav, letter. Most Semitic scripts are abjads, which omit some or all vowels. The Geʽez script of Ethiopia and Eritrea is technically an abugida, and Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin script. The reconstructed word order of Proto-Semitic is verb–subject–object, which Classical Arabic and Biblical Hebrew keep.

Scholars have accepted the similarity of Hebrew, Arabic and Aramaic since medieval times. Guillaume Postel published a comparison of them in Latin in 1538, but did not name the group. The term Semitic was created by the Göttingen school of history, first by August Ludwig von Schlözer in 1781, from Shem, one of Noah's three sons in the Book of Genesis, and Johann Gottfried Eichhorn popularised it in 1795. Classical Syriac, an Aramaic dialect of about 200 CE, became a literary language of early Christianity. Classical Arabic is the language of the Quran, and Maltese descends from the extinct Siculo-Arabic of Sicily.
sendai: Sendai stretches from the Pacific Ocean to the Ōu Mountains, which form the east and west borders of Miyagi Prefecture. Its eastern part is a plain, its centre hilly and its west mountainous, and the highest point is Mount Funagata at 1,500 metres. Unusually for a large Japanese coastal city, the city core stands on a terrace 40 to 60 metres above sea level. The area was inhabited as early as 20,000 years ago, though the history of Sendai as a city begins with Date Masamune. It became a designated city in 1989 and has five wards, whose names deliberately avoid directions.

Date Masamune was unhappy with his previous stronghold at Iwadeyama, in the north of his territories and hard to reach from Edo. Sendai lay in the centre of his newly defined lands on the major road from Edo, and Tokugawa Ieyasu gave him permission to build a new castle on Aobayama after the Battle of Sekigahara. The name had been written with characters meaning a thousand generations, and Masamune changed it to characters meaning a hermit and a platform. The characters come from a Chinese poem praising a palace of the Han emperor Wen, and tradition says Masamune chose them so that the castle would prosper like a mountain inhabited by an immortal hermit.

In 1613 Masamune built a galleon to send an embassy headed by Hasekura Tsunenaga to the Pope in Rome. The embassy established relations with the Holy See, but the suppression of Christianity in Japan frustrated Masamune's plans. The first railway between Sendai and Tokyo, now the Tōhoku Main Line, opened in 1887 and put the area within a day's travel of Tokyo. Tohoku Imperial University was founded in 1907 and became the first Japanese university to admit women in 1913. After the Second World War the city was rebuilt as a transport and logistics hub for the region.

Sendai is the capital of Miyagi Prefecture and the largest city of the Tōhoku region. It is known as the City of Trees, because of the zelkova trees along Jōzenji Street and Aoba Street, and its Tanabata Festival is the largest in Japan. The ruins of Sendai Castle stand on Aobayama, and the Zuihōden is the tomb of Date Masamune. The Ōsaki Hachimangū shaden, built by Masamune in 1607, is a National Treasure. On 11 March 2011 coastal areas of the city suffered severe damage from a magnitude 9.0 offshore earthquake and the tsunami it caused.
seneca-the-younger: Seneca's father, Seneca the Elder, was a Spanish-born Roman knight who had gained fame as a writer and teacher of rhetoric in Rome, and his brother Annaeus Mela was the father of the poet Lucan. His early career as a senator seems to have been successful, and he was praised for his oratory. According to Cassius Dio, the emperor Caligula was so offended by his success in the Senate that he ordered him to commit suicide, and Seneca survived only because he was seriously ill and Caligula was told that he would soon die anyway.

From 54 to 62 Seneca advised Nero together with the praetorian prefect Sextus Afranius Burrus, and he was appointed suffect consul in 56. His satire Apocolocyntosis lampoons the deification of Claudius. Tacitus and Dio suggest that Nero's early rule, while he listened to Seneca and Burrus, was quite competent. After Burrus died in 62 Seneca's influence declined rapidly, and Tacitus reports that Nero refused his requests to retire in 62 and 64. He lived quietly on his country estates, rarely visiting Rome.

Seneca wrote mostly on ethics, with one work, Naturales Quaestiones, on the physical world. Many upper-class Romans found in Stoicism an ethical framework for political involvement. He was once regarded as eclectic, but modern scholarship sees him as a fairly orthodox Stoic, albeit a free-minded one. Among his later works are the Letters to Lucilius, which set out his philosophical thought.

His plays are tragedies, and ten are attributed to him, of which probably eight are his. Their intense emotions and grim tone seem the opposite of his Stoic beliefs, and until the 16th century he was often thought to be two people, a philosopher and a dramatist. Many scholars have held that they were written for recitation only, while others think they were meant for performance.

In 65 Seneca was caught up in the aftermath of the Pisonian conspiracy, and Nero ordered him to kill himself, though it is unlikely that he took part. He cut several veins, and his wife Pompeia Paulina tried to share his fate but was saved on Nero's order. According to Tacitus, his age and diet made him bleed slowly, and he also took poison, which was not fatal. The early Christian Church thought well of him, and Tertullian called him our Seneca. In the later Middle Ages he was read mostly through the Letters to Lucilius, and Petrarch quoted him more than any authority except Virgil. His suicide has been a popular subject in art.
senegal: Senegal lies on the western coast of Africa between latitudes 12° and 17°N. It almost completely surrounds the Gambia, which separates the southern region of Casamance from the rest of the country. The landscape consists mainly of the rolling sandy plains of the western Sahel, rising to foothills in the southeast, where the highest point, the Baunez ridge, reaches 648 metres. The Senegal River forms the northern border and gives the country its name, and the Gambia and Casamance rivers also cross it. The capital Dakar lies on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of continental Africa. The dry season runs from December to April, with hot, dry harmattan winds.

Archaeological findings indicate that Senegal was inhabited in prehistoric times and continuously occupied by various ethnic groups. Kingdoms were created between the 6th and 14th centuries, among them Takrur in the 6th century, Namandiru and the Jolof Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries, and eastern Senegal was once part of the Ghana Empire. Islam was introduced by the Toucouleur and Soninke through contact with the Almoravid dynasty, and the Serers in particular resisted it. Between 1300 and 1900 close to one-third of the population was enslaved, typically after capture in warfare.

The Jolof Empire grew more powerful in the 14th century, uniting Cayor and the kingdoms of Baol, Siné, Saloum, Waalo, Futa Tooro and Bambouk. It was a voluntary confederacy rather than a state built on conquest, founded by Ndiadiane Ndiaye, and it collapsed around 1549 after the defeat and death of Lele Fouli Fak at the hands of Amari Ngone Sobel Fall.

The Portuguese landed on the coast in the mid-15th century, followed by traders from other countries, including the French. In 1677 France gained control of the island of Gorée, a minor hub of the Atlantic slave trade. From the 1850s the French expanded onto the mainland under Governor Louis Faidherbe, taking over all the kingdoms except the Serer kingdoms of Sine and Saloum. Senegal became independent in 1960.

Dakar is the capital and largest city, and was once the capital of all French West Africa. Senegal is a semi-presidential republic. French is the official language, ratified in 1960, but over 30 languages are spoken, and Wolof is the most widely spoken, serving as a lingua franca alongside French. The largest ethnic groups are the Wolof, Fula and Serer, and Senegalese people are predominantly Muslim. Griots, whose profession is passed down through generations, have kept West African history alive through words and music. Senegal is a member of the African Union, the United Nations and the Economic Community of West African States.
seoul: Seoul lies in the north-west of South Korea, in mountainous and hilly terrain, with Bukhansan on its northern edge. The Han River roughly divides it into northern and southern halves, and the city proper covers 605.25 square kilometres. Four main mountains stand in the centre: Bugaksan, Inwangsan, Naksan and Namsan. The Seoul Fortress Wall, which historically bounded the city, runs over these heights.

People lived in the area 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Around 4,000 BCE they lived in huts with lowered floors called umjip, and around 1,500 BCE communities began to farm at scale and enter the Bronze Age. After the fall of Wiman Joseon (194 to 108 BCE), refugees went south to the Han River basin, bringing the culture and technology of the Chinese Warring States and speeding the region's entry into the Iron Age.

Baekje, founded in 18 BCE as one of the statelets of the Mahan confederacy, became the dominant local power by the 2nd century CE. Its capital, Wiryeseong, is believed to have lain in what is now south-eastern Seoul, though its exact site is uncertain. In July or August 553 Silla took the region from Baekje, and it became part of the new Sin Province. Later names include Bukhansan-gun under Goguryeo, Namgyeong under Goryeo and Hanseong under Joseon.

Seoul was designed as a capital in the late 14th century, and the Joseon dynasty built the Five Grand Palaces there: Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung, Gyeongbokgung and Gyeonghuigung. In the early 20th century the city was occupied by the Empire of Japan. In the Korean War it changed hands four times and was left mostly in ruins, and it has since been rebuilt and rapidly urbanized.

Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, with about 9.6 million residents. It is divided into 25 districts, called gu. The Constitutional Court of Korea declared in 2004 that Seoul must remain the national capital as an unwritten constitutional custom, though many ministries have moved to Sejong City. Five UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the Seoul Capital Area, among them Changdeokgung, Jongmyo and the Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty.
serbia: Serbia lies in the Balkans and the Pannonian Basin. It covers 88,499 square kilometres including the disputed territory of Kosovo, or 77,589 square kilometres excluding it. It has eight neighbouring countries, more than any other European country except Germany. The Pannonian Plain covers the northern third of the country, central Serbia is chiefly hills traversed by rivers, and mountains dominate the southern third.

Elevation ranges from 2,169 metres at the Midžor peak in the Balkan Mountains to just 17 metres near Prahovo in the Timok Valley. Karst topography is prominent in the Dinaric Alps and the Carpathian Mountains, and the country hosts about 1,500 deep caves.

A hominid jaw fragment from Mala Balanica Cave is believed to be up to 525,000 years old. Around 6500 BCE the Starčevo and Vinča cultures were present near modern Belgrade, and Lepenski Vir and Vinča-Belo Brdo lie along the Danube. The Celtic Scordisci settled the area in the 3rd century BCE and built fortified settlements, including Singidunum (present-day Belgrade) and Naissos (present-day Niš). The Romans conquered much of the territory from the 2nd century BCE, and some historians believe 18 Roman emperors were born there, among them Constantine the Great.

Slavs migrated into Byzantine territory in large numbers by the 6th century. The first Serbian proto-state was established in the 7th century and had become a more stable principality by the beginning of the 9th century, remaining a Byzantine vassal state throughout. It was conquered and annexed by the Byzantine Empire in the late 10th century. The Serbian Kingdom lasted from 1217 to 1346, followed by the Serbian Empire from 1346 to 1371 and the Serbian Despotate from 1402 to 1459.

Serbia is a parliamentary republic under a constitution adopted in 2006, after the dissolution of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. The National Assembly has 250 deputies elected for four years. The 2022 census counted a population of 6,647,003, excluding Kosovo, of whom 80.6% were Serbs; Hungarians (2.8%) and Bosniaks (2.3%) are the largest minorities.

The country has five World Heritage sites, among them Stari Ras, the Studenica Monastery and the Roman palace complex of Felix Romuliana, and six traditions on the intangible heritage list, including the slava and kolo dance. Its cultural identity was shaped by its position as a frontier between the Byzantine Empire and Western Christianity, and later between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires.
sergei-eisenstein: Sergei Mikhailovich Eisenstein was born on 22 January 1898 in Riga, then in the Russian Empire, to a middle-class family. His father, the architect Mikhail Osipovich Eisenstein, came from a Jewish family but had converted to the Russian Orthodox Church before his marriage in 1897. His mother took Sergei to Saint Petersburg in 1905. He was raised an Orthodox Christian and later became an atheist. At the Petrograd Institute of Civil Engineering he studied architecture and engineering, but in 1918 he left to join the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. In Minsk in 1920 he saw Kabuki theatre and studied Japanese, learning about 300 kanji characters, which he cited as an influence on his pictorial development.

In 1920 Eisenstein moved to Moscow and worked in the theatre for Proletkult, an experimental institution that aimed at a revolutionary working-class aesthetic. In 1923 he began as a theorist with the essay The Montage of Attractions. His first full-length film was Strike in 1925, followed in the same year by Battleship Potemkin, which was acclaimed around the world, and by October: Ten Days That Shook the World, made for the tenth anniversary of the Revolution. His attention to camera angles, crowd movements and montage drew criticism in the Soviet film community and led to self-criticism and promises to conform to socialist realism.

In 1930 Paramount Pictures gave him a short contract in Hollywood, but his projects failed to impress the studio and it ended by mutual consent. He then made a film in Mexico, Que viva Mexico, financed by the author Upton Sinclair and other investors. It ran far beyond the three or four months agreed, and Sinclair shut down production, leaving the footage in the United States, where others edited it into films that Eisenstein never saw. Alexander Nevsky, made in 1938 with music by Sergei Prokofiev, was received well in the Soviet Union and the West and won him the Order of Lenin and the Stalin Prize.

During the war he worked on the film about Tsar Ivan IV, with Prokofiev scoring it. Ivan the Terrible, Part I won a Stalin Prize. Part II was criticized by various authorities and went unreleased until 1958, and the footage of the unfinished Part III was confiscated and mostly destroyed.

Eisenstein suffered a heart attack on 2 February 1946 and died of a second on 11 February 1948, aged 50. His ashes were buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow. He was a pioneer in the theory and practice of montage.
sergipe: Sergipe covers 21,910 square kilometres and borders Bahia to the south and west and Alagoas to the north. The São Francisco River forms its northern boundary. Inland the state is almost entirely savanna, called caatinga, while the coastline has mangroves, swamps and sandy beaches. The rivers that drain the southern half into the Atlantic are obstructed by sandbars at their mouths, so there are no good ports on the coast. The name comes from an Old Tupi word meaning in the river of the siri, a species of crab.

The region was home to numerous Indigenous peoples, including the Kanindé, the Aratus and the Tupi. Gaspar de Lemos briefly landed there in 1501, and the Portuguese Crown declared it part of the Captaincy of Bahia. It was one of the last coastal regions of Brazil whose Indigenous population resisted Portuguese rule, and it was fully brought under it after about two decades of warfare, during which thousands of Indigenous people were killed and thousands more enslaved to work on sugar plantations. The first Portuguese settlement was at São Cristóvão, then called Sergipe D'El-Rey.

Sergipe was invaded several times by the Dutch and often raided by French buccaneers, who were drawn by its king-wood, a prized commodity. The territory belonged to Dutch-controlled Brazil until the Portuguese regained control in 1645. By 1723 Sergipe, still part of Bahia, produced a third of Bahia's sugar. Land unsuitable for sugarcane was used for livestock, and Sergipe supplied draft animals to farms in Bahia and Pernambuco.

John VI of Portugal signed a decree separating Sergipe from Bahia on 8 July 1820. It kept its separation after the independence of Brazil in 1822, first as a captaincy and then as a province. On 17 March 1855 the provincial president moved the capital from São Cristóvão, inland, to Aracaju on the coast. Sergipe became a state when the Republic of Brazil was proclaimed in 1892.

Sergipe is the smallest Brazilian state by area, larger only than the Federal District, with Aracaju as its capital and largest city. São Cristóvão, the fourth oldest town in the country and the state capital until 1855, has a main square, São Francisco Square, that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
sesame: Sesame, Sesamum indicum, is a plant also called benne. Most of the other species of its genus are wild and native to sub-Saharan Africa, while the cultivated type originated in India. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, and its epithet means of India. The seeds, which are white or black and grow in pods, have one of the highest oil contents of any seed. The plant tolerates drought and heat and will grow where other crops fail, so subsistence farmers at the edge of deserts have grown it. The word sesame comes through Latin and Greek from ancient Semitic languages such as the Akkadian šamaššamu.

Sesame is considered the oldest oilseed crop known to humanity. Charred remains dated to about 3500 to 3050 BCE show that it was domesticated in the Indian subcontinent at least 5,500 years ago. The archaeobotanist Dorian Q. Fuller states that sesame was traded between Mesopotamia and the Indian subcontinent by 2000 BCE, and the Indus Valley civilization may have exported sesame oil to Mesopotamia, where it was called ilu in Sumerian and ellu in Akkadian. Some believe it may instead have originated in Ethiopia.

Egyptians called it sesemt, and it appears in the list of medicinal drugs of the Ebers Papyrus of about 1550 BCE. Baskets of sesame were found among the grave goods of King Tutankhamen, which suggests it was present in Egypt by 1350 BCE. It was grown and pressed for oil at least by 750 BCE in the empire of Urartu.

The seeds are a common ingredient in many cuisines, made into tahini paste and halva in the Middle East and a part of the spice mixture za'atar. Enslaved West Africans brought sesame to colonial America in the 17th century and grew it as a subsistence crop. In Southern Italian cuisine sesame sweets such as giurgiulena remain from the Arabic period. In the early twentieth century sesame oil was a compulsory ingredient of margarine in Europe, because its presence made it simple to detect margarine used to adulterate butter. Around 1920 Burma exported about 197,400 tons of the oil a year.
sevastopol: Sevastopol lies at the south-western tip of the Crimean Peninsula, on the Heracles Peninsula, on the coast of the Black Sea. Much of the city is gathered around the long Bay of Sevastopol, and its navigable harbours made it an important port and naval base throughout its history. Its name joins the Greek sebastós, venerable, and pólis, city, and probably honours Empress Catherine II, who founded it. In the west of the city stand the well-preserved ruins of the ancient Greek port of Chersonesos, founded in the 5th century BCE by settlers from Heraclea Pontica.

Sevastopol was founded in June 1783, in the area of the ruined Greek city of Chersonesus, as a base for a naval squadron under the name Akhtiar, White Cliff, by Rear Admiral Thomas MacKenzie, a Scot in Russian service. In February 1784 Catherine the Great ordered Grigory Potyomkin to build a fortress and call it Sevastopol, and Captain Fyodor Ushakov, commander of the port from 1788, carried out the plans. The name Sevastopol was restored on 29 April (10 May) 1826.

In the Crimean War the allies chose Sevastopol as Russia's main Black Sea naval base. They landed in September 1854 and settled into a siege marked by brutal conditions on both sides. The city fell after eleven months, and the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 forbade Russia to base warships in the Black Sea. In the Second World War it withstood intensive German bombardment in 1941-42, in which the Germans used the 80-cm railway gun Schwerer Gustav, and after 250 days of fierce fighting fell to Axis forces in July 1942. The Red Army liberated it on 9 May 1944.

In the Soviet era it was a closed city. In 1954 Sevastopol and the rest of Crimea were transferred from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR. Russia annexed Crimea, with Sevastopol, in March 2014; the annexation is not recognised internationally.

Sevastopol is the largest city of Crimea and a major Black Sea port, with a population mostly of ethnic Russians and a substantial minority of Ukrainians. Because of its military history most of its streets are named after Russian and Soviet military heroes, and hundreds of monuments and plaques recall its military past.
seven-wonders-of-the-ancient-world: After the conquests of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BCE, Hellenistic travellers gained access to the civilizations of the Egyptians, Persians and Babylonians, and began to list the landmarks that impressed them. The ancient Greeks spoke not of wonders but of theamata, meaning sights or things to be seen, so the list was the ancient counterpart of a travel guidebook. Later the word for wonder, thaumata, was used instead.

The first known list of seven dates to the 2nd to 1st century BCE, and at least eight full lists and ten partial lists are known. Diodorus Siculus mentioned only the Walls of Babylon and the Pyramids. The epigrammist Antipater of Sidon, who lived around or before 100 BCE, listed six of the present wonders and put the walls of Babylon where the Lighthouse of Alexandria now stands. Lists by Herodotus and by the poet Callimachus of Cyrene survive only as references.

The seven names now generally given are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. This canonical list was first established in the 1572 publication Octo Mundi Miracula from a combination of historical sources. Two wonders stood in Greece, two in Turkey, two in Egypt and one in Iraq. Five of the seven celebrate Greek construction; the exceptions are the pyramids and the Hanging Gardens.

Only the Great Pyramid survives, and it lost its white stone facing around 1300 when local communities removed it for building. The Colossus, finished after 280 BCE, fell to an earthquake in 226 or 225 BCE, so all seven stood together for less than sixty years. The Temple of Artemis and the statue of Zeus were destroyed by fire, and the Lighthouse and the tomb of Mausolus by earthquakes.

Sculptures from the tomb and the temple are in the British Museum. Scholars debate the nature of the Hanging Gardens and whether they existed. Later lists added Roman and Christian sites, and Gregory of Tours named the Temple of Solomon and Noah's Ark. Wilhelm Heinrich Roscher found 22 distinct places across 18 classical lists in 1906.
seville: Seville lies on the lower reaches of the River Guadalquivir in the southwest of the Iberian Peninsula, in a fertile valley, at an average height of 7 metres above sea level. Its port, about 80 kilometres from the Atlantic, is the only river harbour in Spain. The summers are very hot and dry.

The city is about 2,200 years old. The original core dates to the 8th century BCE, when the site was on an island in the Guadalquivir, and the Phoenicians and the Tartessians called it Hisbaal. It was founded as the Roman city of Hispalis, and after the Islamic conquest of 711 was called Ishbiliyah. It was the seat of the Wali of Al-Andalus until 716, when the capital moved to Córdoba. After the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in the early 11th century it became the centre of the independent Taifa of Seville, and it was later ruled by the Almoravids and the Almohads, who built its main mosque in the 12th century. It was incorporated into the Crown of Castile in 1248.

Following the voyages of Columbus, Seville was chosen in 1503 as the headquarters of the Casa de Contratación, which made it the gateway to the Indies, though ships had to sail about 80 kilometres up the Guadalquivir to reach it. In the 16th century it was one of the largest cities in Western Europe. Worsening drought in the river gradually moved the trade away to the Bay of Cádiz, which received the fleets of the Indies in 1680 and the Casa de Contratación in 1717.

Seville is the capital of Andalusia and of the province of Seville. Its old town contains a UNESCO World Heritage Site made up of three buildings: the Alcázar, the Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies. Its motto, NO8DO, is popularly read as a rebus for the Spanish No me ha dejado, She has not abandoned me.
sewing-needle: A sewing needle for hand-sewing is a long slender tool with a point at one end and an eye to hold the thread. The earliest were made of bone or wood, and modern ones are made of high-carbon steel wire, plated with nickel or gold against corrosion. Needles have come in many kinds for their uses: sharps for general sewing, embroidery needles with longer eyes, quilting needles, tapestry needles with blunt tips for loose weaves, leather needles with a triangular point, and long upholstery needles that may be straight or curved. Sizes are not standardised, and within a class a higher number means a shorter, thinner needle.

The first sewing was probably the tying together of animal skins, with shards of bone as needles and sinew or plant material as thread. The early limit was making an eye small enough not to damage the material. Bone awls from Blombos Cave in southern Africa date to 73,000 to 70,000 years ago, and a point that may come from a bone needle, found in Sibudu Cave, to 61,000 years ago.

Later needles are better dated. A bone needle from Potok Cave in Slovenia belongs to the Aurignacian, 47,000 to 41,000 years ago. Ivory needles about 30,000 years old come from Kostenki in Russia, and 8,600-year-old needles from Ekşi Höyük in western Anatolia. Flinders Petrie found copper needles at Naqada in Egypt from 4400 to 3000 BCE, and iron needles from the third century BCE were found at the oppidum of Manching. Needles apply the wire-making technology that appeared in the second millennium BCE.

Native Americans used needles from natural sources. The agave leaf, soaked until only long fibres and a sharp tip remained, gave both needle and thread. Steel-making from China reached Spain in the tenth century in the form of the Catalan furnace and later Germany and France. England began making needles in 1639 at Redditch, with the drawn-wire technique still in common use, and about 1655 a Guild of Needlemakers was established in London. In Japan the Festival of Broken Needles, Hari-Kuyo, dates back to the 1600s.
sextus-pompey: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius was the son of Pompey by his third wife, Mucia Tertia, with an elder brother, Gnaeus Pompeius, and a sister, Pompeia. When Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, Gnaeus followed their father to the East while Sextus stayed in Rome in the care of his stepmother, Cornelia Metella. After the defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE the two met Pompey on Lesbos and fled with him to Egypt, where Sextus watched his father killed by treachery on 29 September of that year.

He then joined the resistance to Caesar in the African provinces alongside Metellus Scipio, Cato the Younger and his brother. Caesar defeated the Pompeius brothers at the Battle of Munda in Hispania in 45 BCE. Gnaeus died soon afterwards in a last stand at Lauro; Sextus escaped and raised another army in Spain.

After Caesar's death Mark Antony moved that Sextus be recalled, paid 50 million Attic drachmas for his father's confiscated property and given command of the whole Roman navy. He accepted, but went no further than Massilia before returning to Sicily. When the Second Triumvirate began its proscriptions, many of the proscribed fled to him, and after the battles of Philippi in 42 BCE survivors of the party of Brutus and Cassius did the same. With the whole island as his base he built an army and a strong navy.

In 40 BCE his admiral, the freedman Menas, seized Sardinia from Octavian's governor Marcus Lurius. By the Pact of Misenum in 39 BCE the triumvirs recognised his control of Sicily and Sardinia in exchange for keeping the grain supply to Rome open and his pirates in check. The peace was short. Each side accused the other of breaking it, and Menas betrayed Sardinia to Octavian. Sextus defeated Octavian at sea off Messina in 37 BCE.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa spent a winter building and training a fleet near Lake Avernus. He fought Sextus at Mylae in August 36 BCE, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Titus Statilius Taurus invaded Sicily, and after Naulochus Sextus fled to Asia Minor. Captured in 35 BCE, he was put to death without trial at Miletus by Marcus Titius, whom he had once spared, either on Titius's own initiative or possibly on the orders of Antony or Plancus. Plutarch gives him a minor role in the fall of the Republic; Appian treats him as a central figure who might even have emerged as the final victor.
seychelles: Seychelles is an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, with its capital and largest city, Victoria, about 1,500 kilometres east of mainland Africa. The islands lie northeast of Madagascar. The inner islands, 42 granitic and 2 coralline, occupy the shallow Seychelles Bank and hold 54% of the land area.
