Pliny the Elder describes soap as an invention of the Gauls, made from tallow and ashes. In the second century CE the physician Galen described soap-making with lye and rated Germanic soaps the best and those of Gaul second.

During the Islamic Golden Age hard, pleasantly scented toilet soap was produced in West Asia and North Africa, and soap-making became an established industry. Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi gave recipes, and in Syria soap was made from olive oil, alkali and lime and exported to the rest of the Muslim world and to Europe.

In Europe the soapmakers of Naples formed a guild in the late sixth century, and by the 15th century soap was made on an industrial scale in Antwerp, Castile, Marseille, Naples and Venice. In England a soap tax kept soap a luxury until it was repealed in 1853. Industrially made bar soaps became available in the late 18th century, and William Hesketh Lever and his brother bought a soap works in Warrington in 1886, which became Lever Brothers and later Unilever.
sochi: Sochi lies on the Sochi River along the Black Sea, in the North Caucasus of southern Russia. Greater Sochi is elongated along the coast for 145 kilometres and is about 1,603 kilometres from Moscow. It has a humid subtropical climate, with daytime temperatures of 25 to 29 °C in July and August and about 10 °C in January and February. The Caucasus Nature Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies just to the north, and the city has the region's most northerly tea plantations.

The name is the Russified form of a Circassian name that comes from the Ubykh Ş̂uaça, a compound of the words for sea and side, and roughly means seaside or coast. Georgian sources offer another derivation, from the Georgian word for the fir tree.

In antiquity the Zygii, a Proto-Adyghe people, lived in the area under the Kingdom of Pontus and then the influence of the Roman Empire. From the 6th to the 11th century it belonged successively to the Georgian kingdoms of Lazica and Abkhazia, which built about a dozen churches within the present city boundaries; the northern wall of an 11th-century Byzantine basilica still stands in the Loo microdistrict. The Christian settlements along the coast were later destroyed by invading Alans, Khazars, Mongols and other nomadic powers whose control was slight.

Russia occupied the coastline in 1829 as a result of the Russo-Circassian War and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828 to 1829, but the Circassians did not accept Russian control and kept resisting the new outposts. Supplying weapons to them from abroad caused a diplomatic conflict between the Russian and British empires in 1836 over the mission of the Vixen. Lazarevskoye was founded as a Russian military outpost in 1839 and named after Admiral Mikhail Lazarev. The Michael Archangel Cathedral, built in 1873 to 1891, commemorates the end of the Caucasian War.

In the Russian Civil War the coast saw armed clashes among the Red Army, White forces and the Democratic Republic of Georgia. A railway from Tuapse to Georgia, running within a kilometre or two of the shore, opened in 1923. After the Crimean resorts passed from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR in 1954, Sochi became the unofficial summer capital of the country. In 1961 Soviet officials formed Greater Sochi, stretching 140 kilometres from the southern part of Tuapse to Adler.

Sochi is the largest resort city in Russia, with sanatoriums, hotels and beaches along its coast, and it is divided into four city districts. It hosted the Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2014, with the alpine and Nordic events at the ski resort of Rosa Khutor in Krasnaya Polyana.
socialism: The history of socialism has its origins in the Age of Enlightenment and the French Revolution of 1789, although it has precedents in earlier movements and ideas. Pierre Leroux claimed to have first used the word socialism, in the Parisian journal Le Globe in 1832. He was a follower of Henri de Saint-Simon, one of the founders of what would later be labelled utopian socialism. The utopian socialists condemned liberal individualism for failing to address the poverty, oppression and wealth inequality of the Industrial Revolution. Saint-Simon proposed economic planning and scientific administration, while Robert Owen proposed cooperatives.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1847 and 1848, just before the Revolutions of 1848, and called their position scientific socialism. In the last third of the 19th century parties dedicated to democratic socialism arose in Europe, drawing mainly on Marxism. For one week in December 1899 the Australian Labor Party formed the first socialist government in the world, when it was elected in the Colony of Queensland under Premier Anderson Dawson.

Socialism encompasses diverse economic and social systems characterised by social ownership of the means of production, which can be public, community, collective, cooperative or employee ownership. Systems are divided into non-market forms and market socialism, which retains monetary prices and factor markets. In his Dictionary of Socialism (1924), Angelo S. Rappoport analysed forty definitions and found common elements: criticism of the social effects of private ownership of capital, a view that the solution is some form of collective control, and agreement that the result should be a society based on social justice. Major movements include anarchism, communism, the labour movement, Marxism, social democracy and syndicalism.

By the early 1920s communism and social democracy had become the two dominant tendencies within the international socialist movement. In the first half of the 20th century the Soviet Union and the communist parties of the Third International came to represent socialism as a centrally planned economy directed by a state that owns all the means of production, although other trends condemned what they saw as its lack of democracy. The People's Republic of China, founded in 1949, introduced socialism through a state-led economy, land redistribution and the Anti-Rightist Movement, followed by the Great Leap Forward.

Elsewhere reformist social democrats and democratic socialists came to power through the ballot box. In the UK, Herbert Morrison said that socialism is what the Labour government does, while Aneurin Bevan argued that it requires the main streams of economic activity to be brought under public direction. Such governments established mixed economies with partial nationalisation and social welfare, as in the Nordic model.
socialist-party-of-albania: The Party of Labour of Albania, founded by Enver Hoxha, had ruled the country for over four decades. Hoxha's successor, Ramiz Alia, was forced to introduce limited reforms in the late 1980s, and on 11 December 1990 he announced that the party had given up its monopoly of power. It won the Constitutional Assembly election of 1991, the first free elections held in Albania in almost 80 years, by which time it was no longer a Marxist-Leninist party. At an extraordinary congress held from 10 to 13 June 1991 it reorganised itself as the Socialist Party in order to survive in the new system.

Fatos Nano, a man from the intelligentsia, was elected the first chairman. He helped to reform the old communist party and brought it into the Socialist International. In 2004 a faction led by Ilir Meta broke away and formed the Socialist Movement for Integration. On 10 October 2005, after losing the parliamentary election of that year, Nano resigned and was succeeded by Edi Rama.

Under Rama the party formed the Alliance for a European Albania, which united several parties and won the parliamentary election of 2013, returning the Socialists to government after eight years. Running alone, the party won the elections of 2017 and 2021 with 74 seats in each, enough to govern by itself, though it has had the outside support of the Social Democratic Party in parliament.

The party is described as social-democratic. Its platform of 2013 pledged to replace the flat tax with a progressive tax and supported universal health care. It is pro-European, supports Albania's accession to the European Union and its membership of NATO, and regards Kosovo as the country's main strategic partner and ally. It is an associate of the Party of European Socialists. Its emblem is based on the fist and rose designed by José María Cruz Novillo for the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party in 1977, used without that party's official consent.
socrates: Socrates left no writings, and what is known of him comes from others: his pupils Plato and Xenophon, the comic dramatist Aristophanes, and Aristotle, who was born after his death. These accounts often contradict one another, a difficulty scholars call the Socratic problem. Xenophon wrote about him in the Memorabilia, the Oeconomicus, the Symposium and the Apology. How far Plato's dialogues portray the historical Socrates is debated, and some scholars distinguish an earlier, more faithful portrait from a later one carrying Plato's own views.

Socrates was born in 470 or 469 BCE in the Athenian deme of Alopece, to Sophroniscus, a stoneworker, and Phaenarete, a midwife. He had the usual education of a well-off Athenian and served in three campaigns of the Peloponnesian War, according to Plato. He married Xanthippe, with whom he had three sons, and also a daughter of the statesman Aristides. He was indifferent to comfort, owned one ragged coat and walked barefoot, and he criticised both the democrats and the oligarchs of Athens.

The method named for him, the elenchus, is shown mainly in Plato's early dialogues. Socrates asks an apparent expert for a definition, and further questions lead the expert to contradict it. A new definition is then tested in the same way. The discussion usually ends in an impasse, with the interlocutor unable to define what he thought he understood. Socrates frequently proclaimed his ignorance, saying he was sure only that he did not know.

Scholars dispute what the method achieves. In 1982 Gregory Vlastos argued that it could show only that an interlocutor's beliefs were inconsistent. Because Socrates taught no fixed doctrine, later schools drew different conclusions.

In 399 BCE Socrates was accused of impiety and of corrupting the youth. The accusation was brought by a poet, Meletus, with Anytus and Lycon. The trial came after the defeat of Athens by Sparta at the Battle of Aegospotami in 404 BCE and the rule of the Thirty Tyrants, and it probably lasted most of a day. A jury of hundreds of citizens found him guilty. He proposed free meals from the state, or alternatively a fine of one mina of silver, and the jurors ordered his death. Plato relates that he was put to death with hemlock after refusing offers to help him escape.

Almost every philosophical current after Socrates traced its roots to him, among them Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, the Cynics and the Stoics, except the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists. He was considered to have shifted philosophy from the natural world to human affairs.
sofia: Sofia lies in western Bulgaria in the Sofia Valley, at the northern foot of the Vitosha mountain, on an average altitude of 550 metres. It is surrounded by mountains: Vitosha to the south, Lyulin to the west and the Balkan Mountains to the north. It is built west of the Iskar. Its development as a settlement owes much to its central position in the Balkans: three mountain passes lead to the city and have been key roads since antiquity, and Vitosha is the watershed between the Black and Aegean seas. Hot water springs still flow abundantly in the centre.

The area has a history of nearly 7,000 years. A Neolithic village at Slatina is documented. The earliest tribes were the Thracian Tilataei, and in the 500s BCE the area joined the Odrysian kingdom. In 339 BCE Philip II of Macedon destroyed and ravaged the town for the first time. The Celtic tribe Serdi gave the city its name, Serdica; the earliest mention is an Athenian inscription of the 1st century BCE, and according to Dio Cassius the Roman general Crassus subdued the Serdi. The emperor Marcus Ulpius Traianus gave it the name Ulpia Serdica.

During the decline of the Roman Empire the city was raided by Huns, Visigoths, Avars and Slavs. In 809 Khan Krum incorporated it into the First Bulgarian Empire, and it became known as Sredets. In 1018 the Byzantines ended Bulgarian rule until 1194, when the Second Bulgarian Empire took it back. Sredets was a major administrative, economic, cultural and literary hub until the Ottoman conquest in 1382. From 1530 to 1836 Sofia was the regional capital of Rumelia Eyalet, the Ottoman Empire's largest and most important province.

Its population fell from 70,000 in the late 18th century to 19,000 in 1870 and 11,649 in 1878. Bulgarian rule was restored in 1878, and Sofia was selected as the capital of the Third Bulgarian State the next year, beginning a period of intense demographic and economic growth. After the Liberation War, knyaz Alexander Battenberg invited architects from Austria-Hungary to shape the new capital.

Sofia is the capital and largest city of Bulgaria. Ancient Roman, Byzantine and medieval Bulgarian buildings survive in the centre, among them the 4th-century Rotunda of St. George, the walls of the Serdica fortress and part of the Amphitheatre of Serdica. The Boyana Church was included on the World Heritage List in 1979.
solomon: Solomon was born in Jerusalem, the second child of David and his wife Bathsheba, the widow of Uriah the Hittite. The first child of the union, a son conceived while Uriah was alive, died seven days after birth, which the Hebrew Bible suggests was a judgment from God. Solomon had three named full brothers and six known older half-brothers. His two names, Solomon and Jedidiah, are traditionally taken to mean peaceful and friend of God. The conventional dates of his reign, about 970 to 931 BCE, derive from biblical chronology.

According to the Hebrew Bible, God appeared to Solomon in a dream and asked what he wanted. Solomon asked for wisdom in order to rule his people, and God, pleased that he had not asked for long life or the death of his enemies, promised it. The account describes a reign of forty years in which Israel reached a height of splendour and wealth. He allied himself with Hiram I, king of Tyre, who sent materials and an architect for the Temple that David had gathered materials to build. The account also gives him 700 wives and 300 concubines, many of them foreign princesses, and disapproves of his building temples to their gods. It tells of a visit by the Queen of Sheba.

Solomon died of natural causes at around 55 years of age. His son Rehoboam succeeded him, but ten of the tribes refused him and followed Jeroboam, splitting the monarchy into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the smaller southern Kingdom of Judah. The historicity of Solomon is much debated. Current scholarship generally allows that a historical Solomon is possible, but regards the biblical picture of his opulence as almost surely an anachronistic exaggeration. Tradition ascribes to him the books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs. He is revered in Islam as the prophet Sulaiman ibn Dawud, and the Solomon Islands were named for him by Álvaro de Mendaña in 1568.
solon: Solon's family belonged to a noble Eupatrid clan of Attica. His father was probably Execestides, which would trace his lineage back to Codrus, the last king of Athens. According to Plutarch he was related to the later tyrant Pisistratus. When Athens and Megara contested possession of Salamis, Solon led the Athenian forces after repeated disasters and raised their morale with a patriotic poem. With the support of Pisistratus he defeated the Megarians around 595 BCE, and the Spartans, asked to settle the dispute, awarded the island to Athens.

According to Diogenes Laërtius, Solon was chosen archon in 594 BCE and repealed all of Draco's laws except those on homicide. His debt relief, later called the seisachtheia, the shaking off of burdens, addressed a system in which farmers who could not honour their obligations, and their families, could be sold into slavery. Aristotle's Athenian Constitution calls him the first people's champion, and says he admitted all citizens to the Ekklesia and formed a court, the Heliaia, from all citizens. His laws were inscribed on wooden axones kept in the Prytaneion.

Modern knowledge is limited. His laws survive only in fragments quoted by Plutarch and others, and fourth-century orators such as Aeschines tended to attribute to him every law of their own day. His poems also survive only in fragments.

After completing his reforms Solon surrendered his extraordinary authority and travelled abroad for ten years so that the Athenians could not press him to repeal any law. Within four years of his departure the old social rifts returned, and Pisistratus ended the factionalism by force and established a tyranny. Solon opposed him and died shortly after, around the age of 70. Pausanias lists him among the Seven Sages of Greece, and Demosthenes credited his reforms with starting a golden age.
somalia: Somalia is the easternmost country in continental Africa. It borders Ethiopia, Djibouti and Kenya, and has the longest coastline on the mainland, more than 3,333 kilometres, along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Its land area is 637,657 square kilometres of plateaus, plains and highlands. In the north a semi-desert plain, the Guban, runs parallel to the Gulf of Aden coast, and the Cal Madow range contains the highest peak, Shimbiris, at about 2,416 metres. The country sits at the mouth of the Bab el Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea.

The oldest evidence of burial customs in the Horn of Africa comes from cemeteries in Somalia dating to the 4th millennium BCE. The Laas Geel rock art near Hargeisa is approximately 5,000 years old. Ancient stone ruins have been taken as evidence of a civilisation that traded with Egypt and Mycenaean Greece from the second millennium BCE, supporting the hypothesis that Somalia or adjacent regions were the Land of Punt. An Egyptian expedition to Punt sent by Queen Hatshepsut is recorded on the reliefs at Deir el-Bahari. Puntites traded myrrh, spices, gold, ebony, ivory and frankincense.

In the Middle Ages the Ajuran Sultanate, Adal Sultanate and Sultanate of the Geledi dominated regional trade. The Italian and British empires colonised the sultanates in the late 19th century, forming Italian Somaliland and British Somaliland, which united in 1960 as the Somali Republic. Siad Barre seized power in 1969, launched a failed invasion of Ethiopia and brutally attempted to quash the Somaliland War of Independence.

Barre's regime collapsed in 1991 with the onset of the Somali Civil War. A provisional constitution adopted on 1 August 2012 made Somalia a federation. About 85 per cent of residents are ethnic Somalis. Somali is the official language, Arabic is recognised as a second, and the overwhelming majority are Sunni Muslims. About 80 per cent of the population are nomadic or semi-nomadic pastoralists.
sonderbund-war: In the early 1840s the radical Free Democratic Party of Switzerland, strong in the largely Protestant cantons and among the urban bourgeoisie, won a majority in the Federal Diet, the Tagsatzung, and proposed a new constitution that would draw the cantons closer together. The Diet had also acted against the Catholic Church, closing the monasteries and convents of Aargau in 1841 and seizing their property. When Lucerne recalled the Jesuits to head its education, bands of armed radicals known as Freischärler invaded the canton.

In 1845 Lucerne, Fribourg, Valais, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, all predominantly Catholic and under conservative governments, formed the Sonderbund, or separate alliance. Ticino and Solothurn, Catholic but liberal, stayed out. On 21 October 1847 the Diet ordered the league dissolved as a breach of the Federal Treaty of 1815, which forbade such alliances. Austria sent the Sonderbund some money and munitions, but the great powers could not agree on intervention, which Lord Palmerston of Britain refused to support.

The Sonderbund's commander was Jean-Ulrich de Salis-Soglio of Grisons, himself a Protestant. The Diet's choice, Guillaume Henri Dufour of Geneva, was sworn in on 25 October after first declining the office. Neuchâtel and Appenzell Innerrhoden declared themselves neutral and sent no troops. The Sonderbund moved first: troops from Uri seized the St. Gotthard Pass in early November, and the first deaths came on 4 November.

Dufour turned first on isolated Fribourg, which surrendered on 14 November; its act of surrender became the template for the other cantons. Zug's parliament voted to give up on 21 November. On 23 November the federal divisions converged on Lucerne. At Gisikon a third assault, led in person by Colonel Eduard Ziegler, carried the Sonderbund position after two hours; thirty-seven men were killed and about 100 wounded. Federal troops entered Lucerne unopposed the next morning. Unterwalden, Schwyz and Uri yielded between 25 and 27 November, and Valais on 29 November.

The federal army reported 78 killed and 260 wounded; later research arrived at 60 dead and 386 wounded on the federal side and 33 killed and 124 wounded among the Sonderbund. Dufour had ordered his troops to care for the injured and declined to use Congreve rockets, so as not to give the war a violent character. The Sonderbund governments were forced to resign, and Liberals took power in Fribourg, Lucerne and Valais. Federal troops left the occupied cantons by February 1848. The constitution of that year banished the Jesuits from Switzerland, a provision lifted by a vote on 20 May 1973.
song-of-songs: The Song of Songs, in Hebrew Shir ha-Shirim, is one of the five megillot, or scrolls, in the Ketuvim, the last section of the Tanakh. Unlike other books of the Hebrew Bible it is erotic poetry, in which lovers express desire, exchange compliments and invite one another to enjoy. It tells a love story between a woman and her lover through dialogues, dreams and metaphors, and the woman warns the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time.

Its title follows an idiom of biblical Hebrew that marks the supreme member of a class, as in Holy of Holies, and the name Song of Solomon means a song of, by, for or dedicated to Solomon. It has no plot, but links between its beginning and end form a framework, and scholars have not agreed how to divide it.

The text gives no explicit reference to its author, or to when, where or how it was composed. Its superscription calls it Solomon's, but modern scholarship argues that it may contain ancient material while there is no evidence that Solomon wrote it. Since the 1800s most scholars have dated it to the 3rd century BCE, chiefly on its language, whose vocabulary, morphology and syntax point to a date centuries after Solomon.

It has parallels with Mesopotamian and Egyptian love poetry and with the pastoral poems of Theocritus, and proposals range from the 10th to the 2nd century BCE; some scholars doubt that its language demands a date after the Babylonian exile. Scholars also debate whether it is a single poem or an anthology, and some connect it with the sacred marriage of Ishtar and Tammuz.

Most scholars now read the Song as erotic poetry celebrating human love, not as a divine metaphor. Judaism accepted it into the canon and long read it as an allegory of the love between God and Israel; canonicity was tied to its attribution to Solomon, and Rabbi Akiva is reported to have forbidden singing it in taverns while defending its place in scripture. Kabbalah later gave it a mystical reading.

Many Jews read it during Passover, a custom first recorded in the 8th century. In Christianity it is viewed as an allegory of Christ and his bride, the Church. It has inspired works by Marc Chagall, Carl Theodor Dreyer, Toni Morrison and John Steinbeck.
sophocles: Sophocles was the son of Sophillus, a wealthy member of the rural deme of Hippeius Colonus in Attica, which later became the setting of his play Oedipus at Colonus. He was probably born there a few years before the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, and 496 or 497 BCE is the most likely year. His father manufactured armour, and he was highly educated.

In 480 BCE he was chosen to lead the paean, a choral chant to a god, for the Greek victory over the Persians at the Battle of Salamis. He lived through both the Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War, and died at the age of 90 or 91 in the winter of 406/5 BCE.

His first artistic triumph came in 468 BCE, when he took first prize at the Dionysia and beat Aeschylus, the reigning master of Athenian drama. According to Plutarch, the archon departed from the custom of choosing judges by lot and asked Cimon and the other generals present to decide. His first production was probably in 470 BCE. For almost 50 years he was the most successful playwright in the dramatic competitions at the festivals of the Lenaea and the Dionysia. He competed 30 times and won 24, and was never placed lower than second. Aeschylus won 13 competitions and Euripides four.

He also served Athens in public office. In 443/2 BCE he was one of the Hellenotamiai, the treasurers of Athena, and in 441 BCE, according to the Vita Sophoclis, he was elected one of the ten generals as a junior colleague of Pericles and served in the campaign against Samos. In 411 BCE he was chosen as one of the commissioners, the probouloi, who responded to the destruction of the Athenian expedition in Sicily. Foreign rulers invited him to their courts, but he never accepted.

Sophocles wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete: Ajax, Antigone, Women of Trachis, Oedipus Rex, Electra, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus. Only Philoctetes, of 409 BCE, and Oedipus at Colonus, staged in 401 BCE after his death by his grandson, can be dated securely. The three Theban plays, Oedipus Rex, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone, were written for separate competitions many years apart, and they are not a trilogy, which explains some inconsistencies among them.

He is known for innovations in dramatic structure and a deeper development of character than earlier playwrights. Aristotle credits him with adding a third actor, which reduced the role of the chorus, though Themistius attributes this to Aeschylus. Aristotle also used Oedipus Rex in his Poetics as an example of the highest achievement in tragedy. Fragments of the satyr play Ichneutae were discovered in Egypt in 1907, and fragments of the Epigoni in 2005.
soren-kierkegaard: Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was born on 5 May 1813 in Copenhagen, the youngest of seven children of an affluent family. His father, Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard, was a devoutly Christian wool merchant from Jutland who was devoted to the rationalist philosophy of Christian Wolff. The figure of Socrates, whom Kierkegaard met in Plato's dialogues, later shaped his interest in irony and indirect communication.

He met Regine Olsen on 8 May 1837 and proposed to her on 8 September 1840, after passing his theological examinations. He broke off the engagement on 11 August 1841, and after she pleaded with him he ended it verbally on 11 October 1841. His journals blame his melancholy, but his precise motive remains unclear, and the broken engagement is generally considered to have had a major influence on his work.

Kierkegaard published some works under pseudonyms, each presenting a distinct viewpoint, as a way of indirect communication. Either/Or, considered his magnum opus, and Fear and Trembling, his central writing on religion, both appeared in 1843. Critics have accused him of playing with viewpoints without committing to one, though he said all his work came from a service to Christianity.

His key ideas include subjective and objective truth, the knight of faith, anxiety, faith as a passion and the three stages on life's way. He wrote, "Christianity teaches that the way is to become subjective, to become a subject." He attacked Hegelianism by parody, though he admired Hegel personally. A dispute that began with an article by Peder Ludvig Møller in December 1845 led him to ask the satirical paper The Corsair to satirise him. His journals run to over 7,000 pages.

In his last years Kierkegaard attacked the Church of Denmark in newspaper articles and in a series of self-published pamphlets, The Moment. The attack began after Hans Lassen Martensen called the dead Bishop Jacob Peter Mynster a truth-witness, which Kierkegaard strongly objected to. He later said his earlier writing had been preparation for it. He collapsed in the street, spent over a month in Frederiks Hospital, refused communion, and died on 11 November 1855. His nephew Henrik Lund protested at the funeral against burial by the official church.

His work was written in Danish and was at first read mainly in Scandinavia, but was translated into French, German and other languages around the turn of the 20th century. Georg Brandes published the first book on his life and philosophy in 1879. His fame grew greatly in the 1930s, when the existentialist movement named him a precursor, and philosophers both theistic and atheistic drew from him the notions of angst, despair and the importance of the individual.
south-africa: South Africa covers 1,221,037 square kilometres at the southern tip of Africa, with 2,798 kilometres of coastline along the South Atlantic and Indian oceans, and it encloses Lesotho. The interior is a large, almost flat plateau between 1,000 and 2,100 metres high, surrounded by the Great Escarpment, whose eastern stretch is the Drakensberg; Mafadi, at 3,450 metres, is the highest peak. The south-western plateau is the sparsely populated Great Karoo, and the well-watered Highveld holds a great proportion of the commercial farmland and the largest conurbation, Gauteng. The country has three capitals: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.

South Africa holds some of the oldest archaeological and human-fossil sites in the world, among them the caves of the Cradle of Humankind in Gauteng, and modern humans have inhabited Southern Africa for at least 170,000 years. The indigenous San and Khoikhoi were predominantly hunter-gatherers, and the Khoikhoi also practised pastoralism; they were largely displaced or absorbed by the Bantu expansion between 1,500 and 2,000 years ago.

The Kingdom of Mapungubwe formed in the north in the 13th century, and the Venda Kingdom in the 17th. The Dutch established the first European settlement at Table Bay in 1652, the Cape Colony. Its invasion in 1795 and the Battle of Blaauwberg in 1806 led to British occupation, and the Mfecane, a period of upheaval, led to the formation of kingdoms including the Zulu Kingdom.

The Mineral Revolution brought industrialisation and urbanisation. After the Second Boer War the Union of South Africa was created in 1910 by the amalgamation of the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies, and it became a republic after the 1961 referendum. The multi-racial Cape Qualified Franchise was gradually eroded, and the vast majority of black South Africans were not enfranchised until 1994. The National Party imposed apartheid in 1948, institutionalising earlier racial segregation, and after a struggle by the African National Congress and others the repeal of discriminatory laws began in the mid-1980s.

Universal elections took place in 1994, and since then all racial groups have held political representation in a parliamentary republic of nine provinces, in which the president is both head of state and head of government. The 2022 census counted Black African South Africans at 81%, Coloured at 8.2%, White at 7.3% and Indian or Asian at 2.7%. The country has 12 official languages and has been called the rainbow nation.
south-america: South America lies entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean, on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean, and on the south by the Drake Passage, and it has an area of 17,840,000 square kilometres. The geography of the west is dominated by the Andes, the longest mountain range in the world, whose highest mountain is Aconcagua at 6,962 metres. The east contains highlands and vast lowlands where the Amazon, Orinoco and Paraná flow.

The continent holds several superlatives: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall, the Amazon is the largest river by volume, and the Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar place on earth. Lake Titicaca is the highest commercially navigable lake. Most of the population lives near the western or eastern coasts, forming what is called a hollow continent.

South America is thought to have been first inhabited by people who crossed the Bering Land Bridge at least 15,000 years ago and moved south through North America. The Monte Verde II site in Chile, suggested to date to around 14,500 years ago, is among the oldest evidence of human presence. Ancient DNA evidence shows that the peopling was more complex than a single migration, with at least three major dispersals. Llamas and alpacas were domesticated in the Andean highlands circa 3500 BCE.

Caral-Supe on the central Peruvian coast, generally dated to around 3500 BCE, was a pre-ceramic culture whose monumental architecture created one of the first cities of the world. Chavín followed by 900 BCE according to some estimates, and its civilisation spanned 900 to 300 BCE, with artefacts found at Chavín de Huántar in Peru. Irrigation systems and widespread fishing helped establish agrarian societies by 2000 BCE.

The continent includes twelve sovereign countries, two dependent territories and one internal territory, French Guiana. Brazil covers a little less than half of its land area and holds around half of its population. Most countries are presidential republics, and Guyana and Suriname are parliamentary republics. It is the only inhabited continent without monarchies, though the Empire of Brazil existed in the 19th century.

The population is estimated at more than 434 million. Spanish and Portuguese are by far the most spoken languages, with approximately 200 million speakers each. Indigenous languages include Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní, which are recognised with Spanish as national languages.
south-asia: South Asia is the southern sub-region of Asia, defined in both geographical and ethnic-cultural terms. Topographically it is dominated by the Indian subcontinent and is bounded by the Indian Ocean in the south and by the Himalayas, Karakoram and Pamir Mountains in the north. Most of it rests on the Indian Plate, which drifted northeastwards from ancient Gondwana and collided with the Eurasian plate nearly 55 million years ago. The extent of the region is not clear cut: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka are commonly included, and Afghanistan often is too, though it may also be classed as part of Central Asia.

Settled life emerged in the western margins of the Indus basin 9,000 years ago and developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished from c. 3300 to 1300 BCE. By 1200 BCE an archaic form of Sanskrit had spread into India from the northwest, and by 400 BCE caste stratification had emerged within Hinduism, while Buddhism and Jainism had arisen proclaiming social orders unlinked to heredity.

Mahmud of Ghazni raided northern India seventeen times between 997 and 1030, and the Delhi Sultanate was founded in the 13th century. The Mughal Empire followed in 1526, while the Vijayanagara Empire and the Kingdom of Mewar remained under Hindu kings and local Muslim rulers held parts of the Deccan. The British East India Company gradually expanded its rule; Crown rule began in 1858. In 1947 the British Indian Empire was partitioned into the Dominion of India and the Dominion of Pakistan, amid large-scale loss of life and migration. East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh after the war of 1971.

South Asia has an area of 5.2 million square kilometres, about 10 percent of Asia, and about 2 billion people, which makes it the most populous and the most densely populated geographical region in the world. Hindus form about 68 percent of its people and Muslims about 31 percent, while Buddhists, Jains, Christians and Sikhs make up most of the rest. The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, founded in 1985 with seven members, brings together the nations of the region.
south-carolina: South Carolina borders North Carolina to the north and northeast, the Atlantic Ocean to the southeast, and Georgia to the west and south across the Savannah River. From east to west it has three natural regions: the Atlantic coastal plain, the Piedmont and, in the northwestern corner, the Blue Ridge Mountains. The coastal plain makes up two-thirds of the state, and its eastern edge is the Sea Islands, a chain of tidal and barrier islands. It has many salt marshes and estuaries, and natural ports such as Georgetown and Charleston.

There is evidence of human activity in the area from about 50,000 years ago. When Europeans arrived, around 1500, there were many separate Native American polities, among them the powerful Cofitachequi. About a dozen tribes of Siouan background lived up the rivers of the coastal plain, the Cherokee further west and the Catawba along the Catawba River. They lived in villages and relied on agriculture.

The Spanish were the first Europeans in the area. On 8 October 1526 they founded San Miguel de Gualdape near present-day Georgetown, the first European settlement in what is now the contiguous United States. It began with five hundred settlers and was abandoned eight months later by one hundred and fifty survivors. In 1540 Hernando de Soto explored the region and the main town of Cofitachequi.

The state is named for King Charles I of England, who first formed the English colony, Carolus being Latin for Charles. The Province of South Carolina was formed in 1712 and became a royal colony in 1719. More than 200 battles and skirmishes of the Revolutionary War were fought within it, and it ratified the United States Constitution on 23 May 1788, the eighth state to do so. As a slave state it was the first to vote for secession, in 1860, and it was readmitted to the Union in 1868. The civil rights movement of the mid-twentieth century helped end segregation and legal discrimination in the state.

South Carolina is composed of 46 counties. Its capital is Columbia and its most populous city is Charleston. A Gullah community lives in the state, and the Catawba Indian Nation is its one federally recognised tribe.
south-china-sea: The South China Sea is bounded in the north by South China, in the west by the Indochinese Peninsula, in the east by Taiwan and the north-western Philippines, and in the south by Borneo, eastern Sumatra and the Bangka Belitung Islands. It covers around 3,500,000 square kilometres and connects with the East China Sea through the Taiwan Strait and with the Philippine Sea through the Luzon Strait. Its average depth is 1,212 metres. Major rivers flowing into it include the Pearl, the Red and the Mekong.

The sea lies above a drowned continental shelf, and during recent ice ages, when sea level was hundreds of metres lower, Borneo was part of the Asian mainland. The basin opened around 45 million years ago, when the so-called Dangerous Ground rifted away from southern China, and extension ceased around 17 million years ago.

The sea has long been a trade route between north-east Asia, China, Southeast Asia, India and the West. Many trading-ship wrecks on its floor attest to commerce going back centuries, and nine historic ships carrying ceramics dating from the 10th to the 19th century were excavated under the Swedish engineer Sten Sjöstrand.

The names for the sea reflect its users. The Yi Zhou Shu, a chronicle of the Western Zhou dynasty, gives the first Chinese name, Nanfang Hai, the Southern Sea, and says that people from the sea sent tribute of hawksbill sea turtles to the Zhou rulers. In Southeast Asia it was once called the Champa Sea, after the maritime kingdom of Champa, which flourished there before the 16th century. Portuguese sailors in the 16th century called it the China Sea. Most of the sea came under Japanese naval control during World War II, after Japan took many surrounding territories in 1941.

The sea contains over 250 small islands, atolls, cays, shoals and reefs, most without indigenous people and many covered at high tide. They include the Spratly Islands, the Paracel Islands, Pratas Island, Macclesfield Bank and Scarborough Shoal. The largest of the Spratlys, Taiping Island, is just over 1.3 kilometres long. Several states border or claim parts of the sea, and the claims are reflected in the variety of names for it.
south-korea: The Korean Peninsula was inhabited as early as the Lower Paleolithic. According to Korea's founding mythology, the history of Korea begins with the founding of Gojoseon in 2333 BCE by Dangun; Chinese records note Gojoseon in the early 7th century BCE. In 108 BCE the Han dynasty defeated Wiman Joseon and installed four commanderies in the north of the peninsula. The Lelang commandery remained a centre of cultural and economic exchange for four centuries, until Goguryeo conquered it in 313 CE.

From the Proto-Three Kingdoms states of Buyeo, Okjeo, Dongye and Samhan emerged the Three Kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla. Goguryeo was the largest and a highly militaristic state, with 700 years of history. Under Gwanggaeto the Great and his son Jangsu it subdued Baekje and Silla. In the Goguryeo-Sui War it is said to have defeated a force of over a million men.

The Goryeo dynasty (918 to 1392) achieved lasting unification, and the Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1897) followed it, maintaining an isolationist policy from the mid-17th century. The Korean Empire (1897 to 1910) was annexed by the Empire of Japan in 1910. After Japan's surrender in World War II, Korea was divided into a Soviet-occupied northern zone and a United States-occupied southern zone, and the Republic of Korea was established in August 1948.

The Korean War began in 1950 with a North Korean invasion and ended in 1953 with an armistice, with three million Koreans dead and both economies in ruins. No peace treaty was signed. South Korea then endured a series of dictatorships punctuated by coups, revolutions and violent uprisings, while its economy grew rapidly and it became one of the Four Asian Tigers. The June Democratic Struggle of 1987 ended authoritarian rule and led to the Sixth Republic.

Under the 1987 constitution South Korea is a unitary presidential republic with a unicameral National Assembly. It is divided into ten provinces, three special self-governing provinces and several cities with special status. Its recorded economic growth was among the fastest between the early 1960s and the late 1990s; South Koreans call this the Miracle on the Han River.

The population was roughly 51.7 million in 2022. South Korea shares its traditional culture with North Korea, though the two have developed distinct contemporary cultures since 1945. It has 16 World Heritage Sites.
south-ossetia: South Ossetia is a very mountainous region in the Caucasus. It occupies the southern slopes of the Greater Caucasus range and its foothills, which form part of the Iberia Plain, and the Likhi Range marks its western boundary. The Greater Caucasus forms its northern border with Russia, and the only main road across the range, the Transkam highway through the Roki Tunnel, was completed in 1986. The mountains shield it from cold air from the north, so it is warmer there than in the Northern Caucasus.

The Ossetians are believed to descend from the Alans, a nomadic Iranian people whose kingdom of Alania emerged in the northern Caucasus in the 8th century. Alania fell to a Mongol invasion and later to the armies of Timur, who massacred much of its population, and surviving Alans retreated into the central Caucasus and gradually migrated south into the Kingdom of Georgia. In 1306, after a three-month siege of Gori, George V of Georgia took Gori and the territory of South Ossetia from them. Georgian historians place the mass migration of Ossetians into Georgia in the 17th century, while Ossetian historians say they lived there since ancient times.

After the Russian Revolution the area became part of the Democratic Republic of Georgia. In 1918 conflict began between landless Ossetian peasants, influenced by Bolshevism, and the ethnic Georgian aristocrats who owned the land. The first Ossetian rebellion began in February 1918, and further uprisings in 1919 and 1920, covertly supported by Soviet Russia, were defeated. Ossetian sources allege that the crushing of the 1920 uprising killed 5,000 Ossetians, with more than 13,000 further deaths from hunger and epidemics.

Soviet authorities established the South Ossetian Autonomous Oblast in 1922, and it declared independence from the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic in September 1990. Georgia abolished its autonomy and sent troops, which led to the 1991–1992 South Ossetia War, with Russian involvement on the Ossetian side. Escalations in 2004 and in the Russo-Georgian War of August 2008 left Ossetian and Russian forces in full de facto control of the former oblast.

South Ossetia's status is disputed. Russia recognised it as independent after the 2008 war, while Georgia and most other states regard it as Georgian territory under Russian occupation. Its capital is Tskhinvali, and it has the official names Republic of South Ossetia and State of Alania, which the 2017 referendum gave equal standing.
south-sudan: South Sudan lies between latitudes 3° and 13°N and is covered in tropical forest, swamps and grassland. The Nile river system runs south to north across its centre. The White Nile, known locally as the Bahr al Jabal, passes Juba and forms the Sudd, a large swamp of seasonally flooded grassland. Habitats include plateaus, savannahs, floodplains and wetlands, and Bandingilo National Park hosts one of the largest wildlife migrations in the world.

The Nilotic peoples of the region, among them the Dinka, Anyuak, Bari, Acholi, Nuer and Shilluk, first entered South Sudan sometime before the tenth century. From the 15th to the 19th century migrations, largely from the area of Bahr el Ghazal, brought the Anyuak, Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk to their modern locations, while the Acholi and Bari settled in Equatoria. The Zande and others, who entered in the 16th century, established the region's largest state, in Equatoria. In the 18th century the Avungara sib rose to power over the rest of Azande society.

Egypt under Khedive Ismail Pasha first tried to control the region in the 1870s, setting up the province of Equatoria; its governors were Samuel Baker from 1869, Charles George Gordon from 1874 and Emin Pasha from 1878. Sudan was governed as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium from 1899 until independence in 1956. British policies favouring Christian missionaries, such as the Closed District Ordinance of 1922, together with the swamplands along the White Nile, limited the spread of Islam to the south. Colonial policy emphasised the development of the Arabised north and largely ignored the south, which lacked schools, hospitals, roads and bridges.

After Sudan's first independent elections in 1958, continued neglect of the south by the Khartoum government led to revolts and the longest civil war on the continent. Following the First Sudanese Civil War the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region was formed in 1972 and lasted until 1983, when the Second Sudanese Civil War began. It ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005, and southern autonomy was restored. More than 2 million people are said to have died in the wars and more than 4 million were displaced. South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after 98.8% voted for independence in a referendum in January 2011.

South Sudan is a landlocked country in East Africa, and its capital and largest city is Juba. Its transitional constitution, in force since 9 July 2011, sets up a presidential system with a two-house National Legislature. The population is composed mostly of Nilotic peoples, the Dinka being the largest group, followed by the Nuer and the Azande. The common languages are Juba Arabic and English. A civil war was fought from 2013 to 2018.
southampton: Archaeological finds suggest the area has been inhabited since the Stone Age. After the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 and the conquest of the local Britons in 70, a fortress settlement named Clausentum was established at the site of modern Bitterne Manor. It was an important trading port and defensive outpost of Winchester, defended by a wall and two ditches, and is thought to have had a bath house. Clausentum was not abandoned until around 410.

After the Norman Conquest of 1066 Southampton became the major port of transit between Winchester, then the capital of England, and Normandy. Southampton Castle was built in the 12th century, and the surviving remains of merchants' houses such as King John's House and Canute's Palace show the wealth of the town at that time. By the 13th century it was a leading port, importing French wine in exchange for English cloth and wool. French pirates raided it, which led to the building of the fortified town walls, many of which still stand.

In 1415, before Henry V left for the Battle of Agincourt, the ringleaders of the Southampton Plot, Richard, Earl of Cambridge, Henry Scrope, 3rd Baron Scrope of Masham, and Sir Thomas Grey of Heton, were accused of high treason, tried at what is now the Red Lion public house in the High Street and executed outside the Bargate. The friary was dissolved in 1538. The Pilgrim Fathers set out from the port aboard the Mayflower in 1620, though the ship was forced to return to Plymouth. In 1642, during the English Civil War, a Parliamentary garrison moved in, and the Royalists, who advanced as far as Redbridge in March 1644, were prevented from taking the town.

The town expanded greatly in the Victorian era. The Southampton Docks company was formed in 1835, the foundation stone of the docks was laid in October 1838, the first dock opened in 1842, and the railway link to London was fully opened in May 1840. It became known as The Gateway to the Empire. In 1912 the RMS Titanic sailed from Southampton; 497 men, four in five of the crew on board, were Sotonians. The city was heavily bombed in the Second World War and was a major embarkation point for D-Day. Southampton acquired city status in 1964, had a population of 248,922 at the 2021 census, and has the longest surviving stretch of medieval walls in England.
southeast-asia: Southeast Asia lies south of China, east of the Indian subcontinent and northwest of mainland Australia. It divides into Mainland Southeast Asia and Maritime Southeast Asia, covers about 4,500,000 square kilometres, and has mostly a hot, humid tropical climate shaped by monsoons. It lies near the meeting of geological plates, and Indonesia is one of the most volcanically active places in the world. Europeans long called it the East Indies, and Chinese sources called it Nanyang, the Southern Ocean.

Homo erectus lived in the region about 1,500,000 years ago. Rock art in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo, dated to 40,000 to 60,000 years ago, is currently the oldest known. Contact with the Indian subcontinent from about 400 BCE began a gradual Indianisation: traders and religious figures brought religions, architecture and political administration, and Sanskrit and Pali became the elite languages. Northern Vietnam was never fully Indianised, having been under Chinese rule from 111 BCE to 938 CE.

Islam reached the region through trade from the eighth century but spread widely only later. The Sultanate of Kedah was established in 1136, Samudera Pasai converted in 1267, and Malacca became a centre of Islamic study and maritime trade. Southeast Asia was a critical part of the world trading system before Europeans arrived, above all for spices such as pepper, cloves and nutmeg. Spain, Portugal, the Dutch, the British and the French followed, and commercial interests gradually became annexation. Several countries were briefly occupied by the Empire of Japan in the Second World War, and most of the region was decolonised afterwards.

The region has eleven countries, all members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). About 676 million people live there, and Indonesia is the most populous country. Nearly 800 native languages are spoken. Islam is the most practised faith, with about 240 million adherents, concentrated in Indonesia, Brunei, Malaysia, southern Thailand and the southern Philippines. Its culture shows the long influence of India, China, Islam and the colonial powers.
sovereignty: The word comes from unattested Vulgar Latin superanus, from Latin super, meaning chief or ruler, and entered English in the fourteenth century. In classical antiquity the Roman jurist Ulpian recorded that the people had transferred all their imperium and power to the emperor, and that the laws did not bind him. Medieval monarchs were not absolute, for they shared power with the feudal aristocracy and both were constrained by custom.

The concept returned in the late sixteenth century, when civil wars created a craving for stronger central authority. Jean Bodin, partly in reaction to the French wars of religion, argued in Les Six Livres de la République of 1576 that sovereignty must be absolute. Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan of 1651, reached a similar view for a different reason: people must join in a commonwealth and submit to a sovereign power that can compel them to act for the common good.

Sovereignty is generally defined as supreme, independent control and lawmaking authority over a territory, with hierarchy inside the state and autonomy abroad. The notion of state sovereignty contains four aspects: territory, population, authority and recognition. Stephen D. Krasner distinguishes domestic, interdependence, international legal and Westphalian sovereignty. De jure sovereignty is the legal right to rule a territory and de facto sovereignty the ability to do so in practice. Max Weber described it as a community's monopoly on the legitimate use of force. Internal sovereignty concerns the legitimacy of a government, which may rest on the divine right of kings or on a social contract. Sovereignty may be shared, as in a condominium.

In the Age of Enlightenment sovereignty gained legal and moral force as the main Western description of the state, and by 1800 the social contract was widely accepted as a way of establishing it, especially in the new United States and France. In federal systems, constituent states keep some powers independently, and differing interpretations of state sovereignty, tied to the expansion of slavery and fugitive slave laws, led to the American Civil War.

After the Second World War sovereign prerogatives were increasingly limited by European integration and international human-rights norms. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948, and the Genocide Convention the day before. The meaning of sovereignty has never been universally agreed.
soviet-union: The word soviet means council in Russian. Soviets as workers' councils first appeared during the 1905 Russian Revolution and were quickly suppressed. After the February Revolution of 1917, workers' and soldiers' soviets emerged across the country and shared power with the Russian Provisional Government. The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, demanded that all power pass to the soviets, and after the October Revolution they seized power in their name. Following the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War, the Russian Socialist Federal Soviet Republic and its subordinate republics were merged into the Soviet Union in 1922.

War communism involved nationalisation of industry and forced requisition of agricultural production. After a severe economic collapse Lenin replaced it in 1921 with the New Economic Policy, which legalised free trade and private ownership of small businesses. After Lenin's death in 1924 Joseph Stalin emerged as undisputed ruler. By 1928–1929 he had abandoned the New Economic Policy for full central planning, forced collectivisation and rapid industrialisation. Collectivisation is linked to a devastating famine in the 1930s that killed millions. The Gulag was expanded, and the Great Purge of the late 1930s brought deportations, executions and the Moscow trials.

The Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact with Nazi Germany in 1939, and Germany invaded in 1941. The Soviet Union suffered around 27 million casualties, the most deaths of any country in the Second World War. The Cold War followed, and Soviet forces suppressed uprisings in East Germany, Hungary and Czechoslovakia. Mikhail Gorbachev sought reform from 1985 through glasnost and perestroika. After a failed coup by hardliners in 1991, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus seceded, and on 26 December Gorbachev recognised the dissolution of the Soviet Union. All fifteen republics became independent.

The Soviet Union was a federal union of national republics, the largest being the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. The Communist Party governed under Marxism–Leninism through soviet councils, and the general secretary of the party's Central Committee was the de facto highest office. Elections were uncontested. The economy was centrally planned. Its area of 22,402,200 square kilometres made it the world's largest country, with its capital and largest city at Moscow. Culture went through stages: relative freedom of artistic experiment in the first decade, then under Stalin the imposed style of socialist realism, with other trends severely repressed and many writers imprisoned or killed.
spain: Spain covers most of the Iberian Peninsula and has an area of 505,992 square kilometres, making it Europe's fourth largest country. It also includes the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, the Canary Islands in the Atlantic and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa, so that it is a transcontinental country. Mount Teide on Tenerife, at 3,715 metres, is the highest peak in Spain. The Pyrenees form the border with France and Andorra, and the border with Portugal, at 1,214 kilometres, is the longest uninterrupted border within the European Union.

Archaeological research at Atapuerca shows that the Iberian Peninsula was populated by hominids very early, and Neanderthal populations survived in parts of Iberia until around 40,000 years ago. The paintings in the Altamira cave of Cantabria were created from 35,600 to 13,500 BCE. Before the Roman conquest the major cultures were the Iberians along the Mediterranean coast, the Celts in the interior and north-west, the Lusitanians in the west and the Tartessians in the southwest, while Phoenicians, Carthaginians and Greeks established trading settlements. The Roman conquest created the province of Hispania. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the Visigoths established a kingdom centred on Toledo.

In the early 8th century the Umayyad Caliphate conquered most of the peninsula, with Al-Andalus centred on Córdoba. The northern Christian kingdoms launched the so-called Reconquista, which culminated with the fall of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada.

The union of the Crown of Castile and the Crown of Aragon in 1479 under the Catholic Monarchs is often seen as the de facto unification of Spain as a nation state. During the Age of Discovery Spain led the exploration and conquest of the New World, completed the first circumnavigation of the globe and established one of the largest empires in history. The 19th century brought the Peninsular War of 1808 to 1814 and the loss of most American colonies, and the Spanish Civil War of 1936 to 1939 was followed by the Francoist dictatorship until 1975.

Spain had a population of 49,570,725 in 2026, with Madrid as the capital and largest city. A national referendum on 6 December 1978 approved the new constitution with 88% of voters, and Spain transitioned from a one-party personalist dictatorship to a multiparty parliamentary democracy of seventeen autonomous communities and two autonomous cities. It is a parliamentary monarchy with King Felipe VI as head of state. Spain joined the European Economic Community in 1986 and took part in the launch of the euro in 1999.
spanish-civil-war: Spain had known instability since the overthrow of Queen Isabella II in 1868. The short-lived First Republic of 1873 was overthrown in 1874 and the monarchy restored under Alfonso XII; in 1923 a coup brought Miguel Primo de Rivera to power, and he resigned in January 1930. The Second Republic that followed had broad support, but according to one historian plans for a counter-revolution were already discussed on the day it was proclaimed, and by March 1934 the conspirators had won the agreement of Benito Mussolini to aid a future coup. After the Popular Front won the election of 1936, officers began to plan a rising, with General Emilio Mola as the chief planner.

The coup began in Spanish Morocco on 18 July 1936 and in Spain proper a day later. It was meant to be swift but succeeded only in part: the rebels failed to take any major city except Seville, which gave a landing point for Franco's African troops, and the conservative Catholic areas of Old Castile, León and Galicia fell quickly, leaving Spain divided. Francisco Franco became the supreme leader of the Nationalists on 1 October 1936. In the Republican zone the arming of workers' movements led to a social revolution, especially in Aragon and Catalonia.

Italy sent about 50,000 men and Germany its Condor Legion to the Nationalists, while the Soviet Union and Mexico supported the Republic and tens of thousands of foreign volunteers joined the International Brigades. The United Kingdom, France and the United States followed non-intervention.

The Nationalists captured most of the northern coast in 1937 and took Málaga on 8 February. Republicans took Teruel in January 1938 and lost it again by 22 February, and the Aragon Offensive reached the Mediterranean by 14 April, cutting the Republican zone in two. Franco's troops conquered Catalonia in the first two months of 1939, taking Barcelona on 26 January. On 5 March Colonel Segismundo Casado led a coup against the Republican government to seek peace, which Franco refused. Franco entered Madrid and declared victory on 1 April 1939.

Hundreds of thousands of Republican supporters fled Spain, mostly to camps in southern France, and many who stayed were persecuted. Both sides committed atrocities: the historian Paul Preston estimates at least 130,000 executed by the Nationalists, while between 38,000 and 70,000 civilians were killed in Republican territory. The total death toll remains disputed, with estimates from 250,000 to 1 million. The Nationalists ruled Spain until Franco's death in November 1975. The war was seen variously as a class struggle, a religious struggle, or a struggle between democracy and dictatorship, and it inspired worldwide passion; George Orwell's Homage to Catalonia, published in 1938, recounts his experience of it.
spanish-language: Spanish evolved from the Vulgar Latin that the Romans brought to the Iberian Peninsula during the Second Punic War, beginning in 210 BCE. Several pre-Roman languages had been spoken there, including Proto-Basque, Iberian, Lusitanian, Celtiberian and Gallaecian. The first documents to show traces of what is regarded as the precursor of modern Spanish date from the 9th century, and the first systematic written use of the language happened in Toledo in the 13th century.

The language takes its alternative name, castellano, from the Kingdom of Castile. The Spanish Constitution of 1978 uses castellano for the official language of the whole of Spain. The Royal Spanish Academy, founded in 1713, called the language castellano from 1713 to 1923 and now prefers español, though it regards both terms as synonymous and equally valid.

Spanish is a fusional Romance language of the Ibero-Romance group, written in the Latin script with the addition of the letter ñ. It has five vowel phonemes and between 17 and 19 consonant phonemes, depending on the dialect. Nouns and adjectives have two genders and two numbers, and there are about fifty conjugated forms per verb. About 75% of the modern vocabulary is Latin in origin.

Other influences on the vocabulary came from neighbouring Romance languages such as Mozarabic, Catalan, Portuguese and Occitan, and from Andalusi Arabic, with about 8% of the vocabulary having Arabic roots. Words from Quechua, Nahuatl and other indigenous languages of the Americas were also absorbed, and French, English and German loanwords arrived in the 18th to 20th centuries. For written Portuguese and Spanish, Ethnologue gives a lexical similarity of 89%.

Spanish colonialism in the early modern period carried the language overseas, most notably to the Americas. It is now the world's second-most spoken native language, with an estimated 519 million native speakers in 2025 and about 636 million speakers in total. Mexico has the largest population of native speakers, with about 130 million.

Spanish is an official language of the United Nations and the European Union. The Association of Spanish Language Academies, created in Mexico in 1951, unites the academies of 23 countries. In the United States, Spanish is the second most spoken language, and over 50 million people were estimated to speak it in 2015.
sri-jayawardenepura-kotte: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte lies next to the urban area of Colombo, which is Sri Lanka's de facto economic capital. The municipal area is bounded on the west by Colombo, on the south-west by Dehiwala-Mount Lavinia and on the south-east by Maharagama. The older village of Darugama lay at the confluence of two streams, the Diyawanna Oya and the Kolonnawa Oya. It was a naturally secure place that enemies could not easily enter, and in the 13th century a local chieftain, Nissanka Alagakkonara, built a kotte, or fortress, there.

Kotte was a jala durgha, a water fortress, in the shape of a triangle, with the marshes of the Diyawanna Oya and Kolonnawa Oya forming two long sides and a large inner moat dug along the shorter land side. It covered nearly 2.5 square kilometres and was fortified with ramparts of laterite 2.5 metres high and 10.7 metres broad. Alagakkonara held the army of Arya Chakravarthy in front of Kotte, while he defeated the enemy's invasion fleet at Panadura. In 1391, after Prince Sapumal conquered the Kingdom of Jaffna, Kotte was given the epithet Sri Jayawardenepura, meaning resplendent city of growing victory. It remained the capital of the ancient Kingdom of Kotte until the end of the 16th century.

The city had a king's palace with walls of quartz and a golden spire, a three-storeyed temple housing the Buddha's tooth relic, a five-storeyed arama where sixty monks lived under a high priest, and a royal cemetery at Beddagana. The Portuguese arrived on the island in 1505 and were initially welcomed by the king, but they had militaristic and monopolistic intentions and gained control of the city by 1565. Unable to withstand repeated assaults by the neighbouring Kingdom of Sitawaka, they abandoned it and made Colombo their capital. Urbanisation restarted in the 19th century, and the archaeological remains were torn up for building materials, some of them ending up in the Victoria Bridge across the Kelani River.

Sri Lanka designated Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte as its new capital in 1977 to relieve congestion in Colombo. The official move was marked on 29 April 1982 by the inauguration of the new Parliament building, which stands on reclaimed land on an island of 50,000 square metres in a lake formed by dredging the marshlands around the Diyawanna Oya. President J. R. Jayewardene declared it open. The Kotte Urban Council became the Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte Municipal Council in 1997. Traces of the old moat and rampart are still visible in places, and the city is the seat of the Education Ministry and the University of Sri Jayewardenepura at Nugegoda.
sri-lanka: Sri Lanka lies in the Indian Ocean between latitudes 5° and 10° N, separated from the Indian subcontinent by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait. According to Hindu mythology a land bridge once joined the island to India. It now amounts to a chain of limestone shoals, and legends claim it was passable on foot until 1480 CE, when cyclones deepened the channel. The island consists mostly of flat to rolling coastal plains, with mountains rising only in the south-central part. The highest point is Pidurutalagala at 2,524 metres, and the longest river is the Mahaweli, at 335 kilometres. The coastline is 1,585 kilometres long.

Prehistory on the island goes back 125,000 years and possibly 500,000. In caves such as Pahiyangala, Batadombalena and Belilena archaeologists found the remains of anatomically modern humans, named Balangoda Man. The earliest inhabitants were likely ancestors of the Vedda people. During the protohistoric period, 1000 to 500 BCE, the island was culturally united with southern India and shared its megalithic burials, pottery, iron technology and farming techniques.

According to the Mahāvaṃsa, a Pāḷi chronicle written in the 5th century CE, the original inhabitants were the Yakshas and Nagas, and Sinhalese history traditionally begins in 543 BCE with the arrival of the semi-historical Prince Vijaya, who sailed with 700 followers after being expelled from Vanga, present-day Bengal. Vijaya is the first of about 189 monarchs described in chronicles such as the Dīpavaṃsa, Mahāvaṃsa and Cūḷavaṃsa.

The earliest known Buddhist writings on the island, the Pali Canon, date back to 29 BCE. The island was known to explorers as early as the Anuradhapura period. The Portuguese reached it in 1505 and established a colony in the sixteenth century, the Dutch later controlled the coastal areas, and the British established a colony by the early 19th century. Independence came in 1948 as the Dominion of Ceylon, and the country became a republic in 1972. A civil war between Tamil separatists and the armed forces lasted from 1983 to 2009.

Colombo is the executive and judicial capital and the largest city, and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the legislative capital. The island has been called by many names: Taprobanā by Greek geographers, Sarandīb by Arabs and Persians, and Ceilão by the Portuguese, which became Ceylon in English. Sinhala and Tamil are the official languages. The Sinhalese form about 74% of the population and Sri Lankan Tamils about 12%, with Moors, Indian Tamils, Burghers, Malays and Veddas among smaller communities. Buddhism is the largest religion, and Sinhalese culture, centred in Kandy and Anuradhapura, and Tamil culture, centred in Jaffna, are the two main traditions.
st-georges-grenada: St. George's is the capital and largest city of Grenada and its main port. It stands on the south-west coast of the island, on a horseshoe-shaped harbour, and is surrounded by a hillside that is the rim of an old volcano crater. The climate is humid and tropical, with a wet season from June to December and a dry season from January to May, which favours the spice crops on which the island's economy rests. Nutmeg is the key crop, followed by cocoa, mace, cloves, vanilla, cinnamon and ginger.

The French colonised the island, then called La Grenade, under Jacques Dyel du Parquet, governor of Martinique, and began with skirmishes that virtually exterminated its native Carib population. In 1666 French colonists built a wooden fortification, Fort Royale, on a promontory overlooking the natural harbour. Work began in 1705 on a star fort on the same site, with four stone bastions, to the design of Jean de Giou de Caylus, chief engineer of the French West Indies, and was completed in 1710. The first settlement, at the eastern edge of the harbour, was named Saint Louis after King Louis IX but suffered from flooding and malaria, so a new town, the Ville de Fort Royal, was built.

When the island passed to Britain the town was renamed Saint George's Town after the patron saint of England, and Fort Royal became Fort George. After the mid-1880s St. George's was the capital of the British Windward Islands. Grenada became independent in 1974, and after a leftist coup in 1983 the island was invaded by US troops. In 2004 Hurricane Ivan damaged some 90 per cent of the island's homes.

Fort George still stands on the promontory west of the harbour, and its buildings are used by the police. The Grenada National Museum occupies French barracks dating from 1704, which later served as a prison and as the island's first hotel; it displays Carib and Arawak artefacts and Josephine Bonaparte's marble bath. The tower of St. George's Cathedral was built in 1818 and St. George's Anglican Church in 1825. York House houses the House of Representatives, the Senate and the Supreme Court.
st-johns-antigua-and-barbuda: St. John's lies in the western part of Antigua, around St. John's Harbour, on a gentle slope east of the harbour. It is the main city of the Central Plain region. Before the town was founded, a small group of houses lined the harbour, then known as the Cove. The flat land around it allowed a large network of roads to converge on the city, and its low coastline is prone to flooding.

St. John's was laid out after the French invasion of 1666, because of the strategic position of the harbour, and an act to build a town there was passed in April 1668. On 16 September 1675 the island's legislature, sitting at Old Road, established six places of trade, one of them St. John's, where the island had traditionally had two. By 1689 the town was as large as Falmouth, which it later replaced as the island's dominant city.

The town was largely spared armed conflict. In 1736 a plan by a St. John's resident, Prince Klaas, to turn Antigua into an independent African kingdom was discovered; he was killed and 132 other conspirators were punished. The scare led to the building of barracks on Rat Island in 1741 and in the centre of the town in 1753. A major fire struck in 1768, a hurricane in 1772 damaged its shipping, and another fire in 1782 broke out in one of the most densely populated districts. In 1784 a night watch was established, and building rules required most public buildings to have brick walls and tiled or slate roofs.

St. John's was the seat of government of the British Leeward Islands until the colony was abolished in 1959. The present Government House was built in the early 1800s. In the late 1800s and early 1900s the city had an elected council, which no longer exists.

St. John's is the largest city of Antigua and Barbuda, with a population of 22,219, and houses the Parliament and the other branches of government. Landmarks include the white baroque towers of St. John's Cathedral, Fort James at the harbour entrance, the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda and the Antigua Recreation Ground, the national stadium. Cruise ships dock at Heritage Quay and Redcliffe Quay.
st-peters-basilica: Old St. Peter's Basilica was the fourth-century church begun by the Emperor Constantine the Great between 319 and 333. It had a wide nave, two aisles on each side and an apsidal end, and it was over 103 metres long, with a large colonnaded atrium. It was built over a small shrine believed to mark the burial place of Saint Peter, and it held most of the popes from Peter to the 15th century. By the end of the 15th century, after neglect during the Avignon Papacy, it had fallen into disrepair.

Pope Nicholas V, who reigned from 1447 to 1455, was the first to consider rebuilding, but little was achieved before his death. Pope Julius II then held a competition, and the design of Donato Bramante was chosen: a Greek cross crowned by a dome inspired by the Pantheon. Construction began on 18 April 1506. One method of financing it was granting indulgences in return for contributions, promoted by Albrecht, Archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg, who appointed the Dominican preacher Johann Tetzel; his salesmanship provoked a scandal and led to the Protestant Reformation.

Michelangelo took over a building site where four enormous piers were rising behind the remaining nave of the old basilica. The dome rises to a total height of 136.57 metres from the floor to the top of the external cross, with an internal diameter of 41.47 metres. On 18 February 1606, under Pope Paul V, the dismantling of the remaining parts of the Constantinian basilica began. Carlo Maderno added the nave and façade, as the Counter-Reformation increasingly saw the Latin cross as the true symbol of Christianity. The basilica was completed on 18 November 1626.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini received the patronage of Pope Urban VIII in 1626 and worked on the basilica for 50 years; his works include the baldachin and the chair of Saint Peter, and he designed St. Peter's Square, built between 1656 and 1667. Catholic tradition holds that the tomb of Saint Peter lies directly below the high altar. The dome greatly influenced church architecture in Western Christendom, from Sant'Andrea della Valle in Rome to Christopher Wren's dome at St Paul's Cathedral in London.
state-protection-authority: The force began in 1945 as the Budapest Department of State Political Police. In 1946 it became the State Defence Department of the Hungarian State Police, the ÁVO, and in 1950 the State Protection Authority. Gábor Péter headed it from 1945 to 1952. László Rajk, the Communist minister of the interior, played a crucial part in organising it, and in 1949 became one of its victims: he was arrested, tried for nationalism and Titoism and executed. On 1 January 1950 the authority was removed from the Ministry of the Interior, made independent and given the Border Guard.

The authority served the Hungarian Working People's Party directly, with little reference to the norms of government, and its actions were not subject to judicial review until the early years after Stalin. It gathered intelligence through a vast network of informants. Secret arrests were followed by periods of torture lasting from 3 to 18 months, after which the public prosecutors and courts were called in to pass sentence.

Prisons and internment camps were placed under its supervision, the most notorious at Recsk, Kistarcsa, Tiszalök and Kazincbarcika. Before 1953 some camps aimed at the eventual death of their inmates through overwork and maltreatment. The first government of Imre Nagy, from 1953 to 1955, greatly improved conditions in the camps and ended these efforts.

In 1953 the authority prepared a show trial meant to prove that Raoul Wallenberg had not been taken to the Soviet Union in 1945 but had been killed by Zionists in Budapest. Leaders of the Jewish community, among them Miksa Domonkos and Lajos Stöckler, and two intended witnesses were seized and tortured. After the death of Stalin the preparations were stopped and the prisoners released in the autumn of 1953. Domonkos died shortly afterwards, mainly from the torture.

On 29 October 1956, during the revolution, the militia of József Dudás stormed the secret police headquarters and massacred the officers inside, and the crowd lynched others. The students' and workers' councils then set up armed patrols to detain members of the authority for their own safety and for later trial.
